After the fall of the Satavahanas, several parts of South India came under the rule of the Chalukyas, whose age lasted for around six centuries. The branch that ruled from Badami (Vatapi) in Bijapur district formed the parental line — the Badami (Western) Chalukyas. The Eastern Chalukyas branched off from them and ruled Vengi uninterruptedly for four and a half centuries; towards the end, they became the descendants of the Tanjavoor Cholas and ruled the Tamil region for another two and a half centuries.

Under Chalukyan patronage, South Indian culture flourished both politically and culturally. Hindu religious culture, which had taken birth under the Ikshvakus and Vishnukundins, reached its blossoming under the Chalukyas. Vedanta literature, architecture and sculpture attained their final, highest form during this period, and the temples the Chalukyas built in Karnataka, Gujarat, Maharashtra and Andhradesa remain storehouses of Chalukyan-style art. Regional languages — Telugu, Kannada, Marathi and Gujarati — all attained new literary form during Chalukyan times.

**The Chalukyan branches and their periods:**

| Branch | Period | Core Territory |
|---|---|---|
| Badami (Western) Chalukyas | 543 – 752 A.D. | Maharashtra and Karnataka |
| Eastern Chalukyas (Vengi Chalukyas) | 624 – 1075 A.D. | Vengi (Andhra) |
| Vemulavada Chalukyas | 750 – 973 A.D. | Northwestern Telangana, as feudatories of the Rashtrakutas |
| Mudigonda Chalukyas | 850 – 1200 A.D. | Areas around Khammam |
| Kalyani Chalukyas | 973 – 1157 A.D. | Belonged to the Badami Chalukya line; ruled from Karnataka |

Each of these branches contributed to the development of its respective region as a regional administrative centre, with its own specialities in art, literature and governance.

Like the history of other South Indian ruling dynasties, Chalukyan history depends mainly on stone and copper-plate inscriptions. Most information on the Eastern Chalukyas comes from copper-plate grants. In Chalukyan inscriptions, historians notice three distinct phases:

1.  **Early phase (Kubja Vishnuvardhana to Vishnuvardhana V):** Inscriptions of this phase name only three generations — the donor, his father and grandfather — with no historically valuable information about victories or the sequence of rulers beyond who succeeded whom.
2.  **Change after Gunaga Vijayaditya (Vijayaditya III):** From his time, inscriptions begin recording genealogy and events in more detail.
3.  **Later detailed inscriptions**, which supply administrative and military information.

**Key inscriptions and what they reveal:**

| Inscription | Date | Significance |
|---|---|---|
| Sataluru grant of Gunaga Vijayaditya | — | Gives the chronology and rule periods of earlier Eastern Chalukya rulers |
| Neelgund inscription | 866 A.D. | Records Gunaga Vijayaditya as a feudatory of Amoghavarsha I (Rashtrakuta), paying tribute to him |
| Sanjan copper plate | 872 A.D. | Records that, unlike other feudatories, Gunaga Vijayaditya personally cleaned Amoghavarsha's walking path |
| Kopparam inscription | 631 A.D. | Pulakesi II refers to Vishnuvardhana as heir-apparent (Yuvaraja) |
| Cheepurupalli inscription | 641 A.D. | Shows Vishnuvardhana had assumed the title of maharaja and ruled independently |
| Aihole (Ayyavolu) prasasti | — | Composed in Sanskrit by Ravikeerthi, Pulakesi II's War Minister; the main source for Pulakesi II's reign |
| Kollipara copper plate | — | Records Arikesari I's victories and administration (Vemulavada Chalukyas); its authenticity has been questioned by some scholars |
| Kuruvagattu stone inscription | — | Issued by Beeragruha (Mahaboobnagar), informs on Vemulavada administrative details |
| Vemulavada copper plate of Arikesari II & Chennur copper plate | 941 A.D. | Record how Arikesari II sheltered Yuddhamalla I and made him ruler of Chennur |
| Karimnagar copper plate | 946 A.D. | Traces Vemulavada developments from Yuddhamalla to Arikesari |
| Kurkyala inscription | 940 A.D. | Written by Jayavallabha (brother of the poet Pampa); records that Pampa wrote _Adipurana_ in 941 A.D. |
| Parbhani copper plate (Arikesari III) | 966 A.D. | Records that his Subahdar built Jain temples |
| Repaka inscription (Arikesari) | 968 A.D. | Records construction of a Jain temple and land grants at Repaka |

**Literary sources:** _Vikramarjuna Vijayam_, written in Kannada by the poet Pampa, is a prominent work of the Vemulavada Chalukya period; it contains a eulogy (prasasti) of Arikesari II and explains his relations with the Rashtrakutas. Somadevasuri, a Jain scholar, wrote _Yasastilaka Champukavyam_ (also called _Yasodhara Charitra_) during the time of the later Vemulavada kings — a key source for the religious doctrines of Jainism as well as social and political details of the age. Somadevasuri's _Neetikavyamruta_ is also regarded as a leading literary source of the period.

Only two donors of copper-plate inscriptions are known from Mudigonda Chalukya times: the **Mogala Cheruvu inscription** of Kusumayudha IV, and the **Krivvaka inscription** of Kusumayudha VI (informs on chronology). The **Narayanagiri copper plate** (1004 A.D.) describes the administration of Chalukya Gonagarasa, who ruled the Warangal region. The **Bezawada copper plate** (892 A.D.) records that Kusumayudha donated Kukiparru village to a brahmin, Potamaiah. The **Koravi inscription** (935 A.D.) is another important source.

**Coins as archaeological sources:** Gold coins bearing the name "Chalukya Chandra," issued during the time of Eastern Chalukya Saktivarma (999–1011 A.D.), have been found in Arakan and Siam. Gold, silver and copper coins circulated during the Chalukyan age. The gold coin was called _gadya_ (weighing 88 grains), with variants such as _Rajanarayana gadya_, _Surabhi gadya_ and _Tyaga gadya_. The silver coin was called _mada_, and _kasu_ was the name used for the copper coin.

**Monuments as sources:** Architectural and sculptural monuments testify to Chalukyan religious patronage across Jainism, Saivism and Vaishnavism, treated with equal favour. Since no temples existed anywhere in India for Brahma, the first of the trimurthis, the Western Chalukyas met this gap by constructing the Nava Brahma temples at Alampur. The Raja Rajeswara temple built by the Vemulavada Chalukyas at Vemulavada became famous as a Saiva temple of the age. Chalukyan architecture attained special significance at Alampur, and the Western Chalukyas also built famous structures at Badami and Pattadakal.

No certain sources establish the origin of the Chalukya dynastic name or their place of origin; different inscriptions offer differing, partly legendary, accounts.

**1\. Chandravamsa/Ayodhya** **Traditions**

*   Some inscriptions state Chalukyas belonged to the Chandravamsa that ruled Ayodhya and came south seeking victory, settling there over time. Modern historians give little weight to this, since Ayodhya was never the capital of Chandravamsa kings in later-attested history.
*   In the **Solanki inscriptions** of Gujarat, it is stated that the dynasty's founder was born from the _chalukya_ (palm) of Brahma — hence the name Chalukya.
*   Bilhana's _Vikramankadeva Charitra_ narrates a variant version of this same "born from Brahma's palm" story: amid sufferings caused by rakshasas, Brahma, while offering oblation to the Sun after hearing Indra's prayer, saw a great warrior born from his palm (_chuluka_) — armoured and strongly built — who came to be called Chalukya, with his descendants named Chalukyas.
*   The **Kautham inscription** of Kalyani Chalukya ruler Vikramaditya V gives yet another version: Chalukyas belonged to Chandravamsa kings of Ayodhya. After 59 kings ruled Ayodhya, they went into exile in South India; after 16 more kings ruled there, that kingdom too declined. Some generations later, Jayasimhavallabha defeated the Rashtrakutas and fully re-established Chalukya authority.

**2\. The "Chalika" tribal-name theory**

*   The word "Chalika" first appears in a third-century C.E. inscription of the Ikshvakus at Nagarjunakonda, describing Khandachelika Remmanaka, a feudatory of the Ikshvakus, as king of Hiranya rashtra (Cuddapah district). If "Chalika" is an old form of "Chalukya," this would read as "Chalukya Remmanaka."
*   Chalukya inscriptions show variant forms of the word — Saliki, Saluki, Chelka, Chelalya, Chalukya — suggesting it was originally the name of a Dravidian-language tribe that later became the dynastic name.
*   Dr. Rice felt Chalukyas may have belonged to the **family of Seleucus in Central Asia**, based on the similarity of the words "Chalukya" and "Seleucus" — an opinion not considered trustworthy, as similarity of sound is its only basis.
*   D.C. Sircar held that the Chalukyas belonged to a **Kannada family** who declared themselves Kshatriyas and had a relationship with the Chulikas of Northern India, though no firm sources support this.
*   The **Ranastapudi inscription** states the dynasty's founder stayed in the ashram of Vishnubhatta Somayaji at Mudivemu agraharam (still existing in Cuddapah district — the Hiranya Rashtra of those times). The **Tummeyanoor inscription** of Pulakesi II similarly calls parts of Kurnool and Mahaboobnagar districts "Chalukya Vishaya," on the model of how tribal/community names (Mulaka, Asaka, Andhra, Mahishaka) came to name their areas of habitation. Historians believe the native place itself became known as Chalukya Vishaya.
*   In Maharashtra, a "Chaliki" caste exists near Bidar, where a village called Chalkapuri and a river called "Chalki" are also found.
*   Chinese traveller Hiuen Tsang referred to Pulakesi II as "**Maharastradhipati**." Based on this and other clues, Durga Prasad Dikshit proposed that the Bidar–Osmanabad region was the Chalukyas' native land.
*   Like the Kadambas, the Chalukyas referred to themselves as belonging to _manvya gothrikas_ and as _haratiputras_. The Chalukya royal names Pulakesi and Bittarasa are also held to belong to Karnataka usage — "Pulakesi" derives from _Polikesi_, meaning "hair at the centre of the head" (a hairstyle seen on ancient South Indian warrior sculptures, called _pulakesi_/_ashtavira_). The Kannada word _arasa_ (meaning king) appears in the names of Vengi and Vemulavada Chalukya kings and in some inscriptions — leading B.C. Sircar and other scholars to conclude the Chalukyas were of Karnataka origin.

* * *

### Background and Founding

The ancestors of the Chalukyas were feudatories of the Ikshvakus (who ruled Andhradesa from Vijayapuri) and ruled Hiranya rashtra in Cuddapah district — their native land. In the first half of the fourth century C.E., the Pallavas overthrew the Ikshvakus and occupied Andhradesa, and the Chalukyas were reduced to Pallava subordination. Resenting this, they tried to become independent; Trilochana Pallava attacked and defeated them.

Mayurasarma, the Kadamba ruler, was hostile to the Pallavas, so he allied with the Chalukyas, and together they fought the Pallavas before migrating into Karnataka and establishing a kingdom at Badami; their royal emblem was the **varaha (boar)**.

The founder of the Chalukya dynasty was **Jayasimha (Jayasimha Vallabha)**, who defeated the Rashtrakutas of Manyakheta. The Undikavatika copper plate of the Rashtrakuta ruler Abhimanyudu names a commander-in-chief called Jayasimha; it is opined this was the same Jayasimha Vallabha whom the Aihole inscription of Pulakesi II names as founder of the Chalukya kingdom. After Jayasimha, his son **Ranaraga** ascended the Chalukyan throne.

### Rulers of Badami Chalukyas

| Ruler | Reign |
|---|---|
| Pulakesi I | 535 – 566 A.D. |
| Keertivarma | 566 – 597 A.D. |
| Mangalesa | 598 – 609 A.D. |
| Pulakesi II | 609 – 642 A.D. |
| Vikramaditya | 642 – 680 A.D. |
| Vinayaditya | 680 – 696 A.D. |
| Vijayaditya | 696 – 733 A.D. |
| Vikramaditya II | 733 – 744 A.D. |
| Keertivarma II | 745 – 752 A.D. |

### Pulakesi I (535 – 566 A.D.)

Son of Ranaraga and founder of the independent Chalukyan dynasty. He raised Chalukyan authority from feudatory status to that of an independent kingdom, defied the Kadambas, occupied Vatapi, and built a strong fort there in 543 A.D., making it his capital. His victories are recorded in an inscription found at Badami (543 A.D.). To proclaim his triumphs, he performed an _asvamedha_ sacrifice. An inscription found at Yeleswaram suggests his kingdom extended up to Nalgonda district. He was the first Chalukyan ruler to assume the title "maharaja."

### Keertivarma (566 – 597 A.D.)

Son of Pulakesi I, as capable and courageous as his father. His wife belonged to the Sendraka royal family. He defeated the Mauryas ruling the Konkan region and the Kadambas of Banavasi, extending his kingdom up to Konkan. He built several palaces and temples at Vatapi (Badami), earning praise from historians as the first ruler to beautify Vatapi as a city.

### Mangalesa (598 – 609 A.D.)

As Keertivarma's eldest son Pulakesi II was a minor at his father's death, Keertivarma's brother Mangalesa came to the throne. He defeated the Kadambas and conquered Revati island (Goa), expanding the kingdom, and held the title "paramabhagavata."

Mangalesa tried to ensure the throne would pass to his own heirs after him, and this triggered a war of succession between Pulakesi II and Mangalesa, recorded in the **Hyderabad inscription** (612 A.D.), in which Mangalesa was killed and Pulakesi II ascended the throne in Saka era 581 / C.E. 609.

### Pulakesi II (609 – 642 A.D.)

The greatest ruler among the Western Chalukya kings, comparable to North Indian emperors such as Chandragupta Maurya and Chandragupta I of the Gupta dynasty. With his rise to power, the "Chalukyan age" is said to have properly begun in South Indian history.

**Conquests and expansion**

*   Conducted several military expeditions and converted the Chalukyan kingdom — until then modest in extent — into a great empire spanning Maharashtra, Malwa, Kalinga, Andhra and Karnataka.
*   His minister for war, Ravikeerthi, described his campaigns in the **Aihole (Ayyavolu) prasasti**, composed in Sanskrit. According to it, Pulakesi II first defeated the Kadamba, Ganga, Alupa, Maurya, Lata and Ghurjara kings to secure supremacy over South India.

**Defeat of Harsha**

*   On the banks of the river Narmada, Pulakesi II fought and defeated **Harshavardhana**, the "Lord of Northern India," becoming the first Chalukyan ruler to check a North Indian emperor.
*   The **Ayyavolu inscription** states Pulakesi II arranged his army most effectively and personally defeated Harshavardhana in this famous battle; afterward, the Narmada river became the recognized boundary between the two kingdoms.
*   After this war, Pulakesi II assumed the title "**Parameswara**."

**Eastern campaigns and Vengi**

*   After settling conquered northern areas under the control of his brothers, Pulakesi II began an eastward military expedition, conquering Kosala and Kalinga and raiding Vengi.
*   Disordered political conditions then prevailing in Andhra land aided his campaign greatly; most areas of Telangana and Rayalaseema had already come under his control, though the lower Krishna river areas were under Pallava occupation and Vengi kingdom was under the Durjayas.
*   Entering via Kalinga, Pulakesi first fought and defeated the Durjayas in the Pishtapuram and Kunala battles and occupied Vengi. His donations in Andhra are known from his Kopparam and Maratoor inscriptions.

**Conflicts with the Pallavas**

*   Pulakesi II advanced to Kanchipuram, the Pallava capital, and in a fierce battle at Pullalur defeated Pallava **Mahendravarma** (C.E. 600–630).
*   When Mahendravarma I died, Pulakesi II again invaded, aiming to bring the Pallava kingdom fully under his control; the Banas of Rayalaseema, in this connection, came under Chalukyan control.
*   Battles at Periyala, Manimangalam and Suramara followed between Pallava and Chalukya forces, with many Pallava areas coming under Pulakesi II.

**Death**

*   During the reign of Pallava Narasimhavarma I (630–668 A.D.), the battles took an extreme turn, and Pulakesi II died at Pallava hands; Narasimhavarma advanced to Badami, diminished its importance, and assumed the title "**Vatapikonda**," in a battle fought in C.E. 642 at Manimangalam.
    
*   Though his royal authority thus ended, Pulakesi II is still regarded as the most warlike ruler in South Indian history.
    

**Other notable facts**

*   The Persian emperor sent **Khusru as an ambassador** to Pulakesi II's court; a painting in the Ajanta caves depicts this Persian embassy.
*   Chinese traveller Hiuen-tsang visited his court in 641 A.D. and recorded that the Chalukyan kingdom was extensive, wealthy and prosperous, and that Pulakesi was a kshatriya commanding a great army.
*   With Pulakesi II's death and Narasimhavarma's aggression, Badami's prestige declined; Pallava armies looted the kingdom and created chaos. His sons — **Adityavarma, Chandraditya, Vikramaditya and Jayasimha** — failed to remain united in defending the kingdom from enemy attacks.

### Vikramaditya (642 – 680 A.D.)

Third son of Pulakesi II. He steadied and saved the kingdom from Pallava attacks, and conquered the Pandya, Chola and Kalabhra rulers who had earlier assisted the Pallavas. During his reign, Chalukya–Pallava conflict continued, and Chalukyan authority was extended up to "three seas." He appointed his brother Jaysimhavarma, who had cooperated in his campaigns, as viceroy of the Lata (South Gujarat) kingdom.

### Vinayaditya (680 – 696 A.D.)

Son of Vikramaditya; ruled the inherited kingdom effectively and peacefully, developing it further. His inscriptions record an invasion of Northern India; he fought many battles and received gifts from the Kalabhra, Kerala, Haihaya, Malwa, Chola and Pandya kings. He was finally killed in the "**Vilande**" battle at the hands of the armies of Prameswaravarman, the Ganga king.

### Vijayaditya (696 – 733 A.D.)

Son of Vinayaditya; invaded with a large army and won against several North Indian royal dynasties. He adopted the Ganga-Yamuna torana and the **Pala flag** as his official emblem. As Vinayaditya had died at Badami, Vijayaditya took up kingly duties in C.E. 696. He built temples at Pattadakal (Kesuval).

### Vikramaditya II (733 – 744 A.D.)

Son of Vijayaditya. During his reign, he confronted the rising power of the Arabs and their attacks in the Sindh region. His contemporary, Pallava **Nandivarma II** (C.E. 695–722), assumed the title "**Pallavamalla**"; the Badami Chalukyas defeated the Pallavas in several battles fought between the two. He defeated the Pandya, Chola, Kerala and Kalabhra kingdoms, and as a mark of victory erected a pillar on the coast of the Southern Ocean. His wives, Lokamahadevi (of the Kalachuri dynasty) and Rajaneetrailokyadevi, had the temples "Lokeswaralayam" and "Tralokeswaralayam" built at Pattadakal in their names.

### Keertivarma II (745 – 752 A.D.) — End of the Badami Chalukyas

Son of Vikramaditya II; the last ruler of the Western Chalukya (Badami/Vatapi) dynasty. During his rule, Chalukyan authority began to decline as he was made to confront many critical conditions:

*   Rashtrakuta **Dantidurga** not only occupied the Ellora region but also turned the Chalukya feudatory kings of Kosala, Kalinga and the Telugu Cholas toward himself.
*   As Dantidurga's power rose and Chalukya feudatories defected to him, in C.E. 752 he overthrew the Badami Chalukya dynasty and established the Rashtrakuta kingdom in Karnataka.

Inscriptions explaining the decline of Badami Chalukya authority — the "**Aviyar rock slab**" and "**the Meraj plates**" — are found in the surrounding areas of Maharashtra.

* * *

Eastern Chalukyas stand among the dynasties that rendered the most valuable service to Telugu culture and literature. Because the Vengi region — lying between the Krishna and Godavari rivers — became their capital area, they are also called Vengi Chalukyas. Among the kingdoms that sprang from the mother line of the Badami Chalukyas, Eastern Chalukyas became the leading one, ruling Andhra land for four and a half centuries (C.E. 624 to 1075) with a highly praiseworthy history. Though considered "non-Andhras" by origin, by settling in Vengi and administering in the local language and with local feeling, they safeguarded Telugu culture — even while dynasties such as the Cholas and Chalukyas, fighting each other for supremacy, turned Andhra land into a battlefield, the Vengi Chalukyas tried to uphold the independence, honour and prestige of Andhra land.

### Establishment and Three Phases of Rule

There were different opinions regarding the exact date of establishment, but as per Vengi Chalukya inscriptions, their rule at Vengi commenced in 624 A.D. Their rule (C.E. 624–1075) is divided into three phases:

| Phase | Period | Character |
|---|---|---|
| First | C.E. 624 – 753 | Peace and tranquility |
| Second | C.E. 753 – 973 | Deadly enmity between the Vengi Chalukyas and the Rashtrakutas |
| Third | C.E. 973 – 1075 | Decline of Rashtrakuta power; emergence of the Kalyani Chalukyas |

Though aggression on Vengi occurred at different times, effective Chalukya authority over Vengi began only from C.E. 624 — when the Badami Chalukya king **Pulakesi II**, after conquering the Vengi region, appointed his brother **Kubja Vishnuvardhana** as viceroy there. Kubja Vishnuvardhana came to be regarded as the founder of the Vengi Chalukya kingdom.

### Kubja Vishnuvardhana (624 – 641 A.D.)

Eastern Chalukyan inscriptions record that he ruled Vengi for 18 years. After becoming viceroy, the Vengi kingdom became independent and expanded. He bore titles such as "**Vishamasiddhi**," "**Kamadheva**" and "**Makaradhwaja**" — the "Vishamasiddhi" title reflecting his fame for subjugating impregnable enemy fortresses.

*   Up to C.E. 631, he ruled Vengi as representative of his brother, Pulakesi II. The **Kopparam inscription of C.E. 631** records that Pulakesi II permitted him to rule independently; his own inscriptions (found at Cheepurupalli and Timmapuram) confirm his kingdom extended from Visakhapatnam in the north to Kammanadu in the south, and that he had declared himself maharaja.
*   From his time, feudatory kingdoms began to form within his territory; he honoured servants who helped him in war by granting them small kingdoms. Among the feudatories, he defeated **Indravarma III**, the Ganga dynasty ruler of Kalinga, and made him his feudatory.
*   The **Timmapuram inscription** praises him as a devotee of Vishnu and as "Paramabhagavata." Even so, he also came to be known as "Kartikeya Kaki" (devotee of goddess Durga). His wife, **Ayyanamahadevi**, favoured Jainism, and built a Jain monastery at Bezawada (Vijayawada) for Jain monks, donating a village for it.
*   Chinese traveller **Hiuen-tsang** (C.E. 600–644) visited and recorded conditions of the time.
*   Pulakesi II made two attacks on the Pallava kingdom during C.E. 631–641; in the last expedition, Pallava Narasimhavarma attacked Vatapi, and historians opine that Kubja Vishnuvardhana took part in support of his brother and died along with him.
*   Kubja Vishnuvardhana was a skilful troop leader, an unrivalled warrior, and capable of subjugating any impregnable fortress — plain, forest or hillock. After him, his eldest son, **Jayasimha I**, ascended the throne in C.E. 642.

### Jayasimha I (642 – 673 A.D.)

Known as Jayasimhavallabha I — the first Eastern Chalukyan king to bear the name "Jayasimha." Chalukya inscriptions record he reigned 33 years. His titles were "Sakala Lokasraya" and "Sarvasiddhi." Though his rule was largely peaceful, the Pulamboor inscription records some battles; he stabilised his supremacy over the Boya kings in the Nellore region.

**Significance for Telugu:** During his reign, an inscription in the Telugu language was issued at Vipparla village (Narasaraopet mandal, Guntur district) — the **first Telugu inscription of the Eastern Chalukyas**, showing that Telugu was already gaining prominence from the time of Jayasimhavallabha I. He ruled with great splendour and died in C.E. 673.

### Indrabhattaraka (673 A.D.)

As Jayasimhavallabha I had no children, his brother Indrabhattaraka came to the throne and ruled for only seven days. In this brief week, he issued the **Kondanagoor inscription**. His titles were "tyagadhanudu" and "makaradhwaja."

### Vishnuvardhana II (673 – 682 A.D.)

Son of Indrabhattaraka. People praised him as "**dharmasastravetta.**" His titles included "vishamasiddhi," "makaradhwaja," "sarvalokesaraya" and "pralayaditya" — the "vishamasiddhi" title showing he had assumed the titles of Kubja Vishnuvardhana.

### Mangi Yuvaraju (682 – 706 A.D.)

Son of Vishnuvardhana II; ruled for 25 years with the title "**vijayasiddhi.**" His inscriptions show he expanded the kingdom from Visakhapatnam to Ongole. He had many wives, and from them three sons and a daughter (named Prithvipori).

### Jayasimha II (706 – 718 A.D.)

Eldest son of Mangi Yuvaraju. From his time onward, **wars of succession began**, weakening the Chalukyan kingdom. As he had no children, after him his brothers **Kokkili Maharaju** (C.E. 718–19) and then **Vishnuvardhana III** ascended the throne.

### Vishnuvardhana III (719 – 755 A.D.)

Brother of Kokkili Maharaju. A fight took place between the two brothers for authority over the kingdom; after ruling six months, when Vishnuvardhana III rebelled, Kokkili fled to the central Kalinga region of Elemanchili. During these disturbances, Boya Kottalu in the Nellore region was taken back under Pallava control. He bore the title "tribhuvanamkusa"; his wife was named Vijayamahadevi. He issued many copper-plate inscriptions.

### Vijayaditya I (755 – 772 A.D.)

His reign is important as marking the entry of the Eastern Chalukyas into their **second phase**. Around C.E. 755, the Rashtrakutas under **Dantidurga** ended the Badami Chalukya dynasty and established a new empire with Manyakheta as its capital (their first place of habitation was Latur village in Hyderabad province).

With the rise of the Rashtrakutas, the Chalukya–Rashtrakuta wars began, continuing for around 200 years and leaving history "tainted with blood"; though the Chalukyas made many efforts to confront the Rashtrakutas — even taking advantage of internal conflicts in the enemy camp — they could not escape defeat, and Rashtrakutas under Arikesari I, who ruled Vemulavada in Telangana, attacked Vengi-trikalinga, so that Vengi was at last made to accept the suzerainty of Manyakheta. Vijayaditya I bore the title "tribhuvanamkusa."

### Vishnuvardhana IV (772 – 808 A.D.)

Son of Vijayaditya I; ruled Vengi, starting his rule as a feudatory of Rashtrakuta king **Krishna I** (as his father had been defeated). When Krishna I died in C.E. 722 \[as per source\], a war of succession broke out among his sons, and **Dhruva** ascended the throne in C.E. 780.

*   In the succession war, Dhruva's brother **Govinda** was helped by Vishnuvardhana IV. Dhruva sent **Arikesari I** (Vemulavada Chalukya, ruling Vemulavada in Telangana) against Vishnuvardhana IV, who had helped Govinda. Arikesari defeated Vishnuvardhana. The **Parbhani inscription (C.E. 966)** informs that Arikesari conquered Vengi and Kalinga.
*   Vishnuvardhana accepted Rashtrakuta sovereignty and gave his daughter **Seelamahadevi** in marriage to Dhruva. But even such political marriage alliances could not end the deep-seated enmity between the two dynasties.

### Vijayaditya II (808 – 847 A.D.)

Also known as Narendra Mrigaraju. He fought endless battles with Rashtrakuta feudatories — the Western Ganga and Vemulavada Chalukyas — staying in the battlefield day and night, sword in hand.

*   When the Rashtrakutas interfered in the war of succession between him and Bhimasaluki, the prestige of the Vengi kingdom suffered; despite this, with the help of Nruparudra of the Haihaya dynasty, he fought 108 battles over more than twelve years against the supporters of Bhimasaluki, and at last occupied Vengi.
    
*   For these victories he earned the **titles** "Narendreswara," "Narendramrugaraju," "Chalukyaraya" and "Vikramadavali."
    
*   Rashtrakuta king **Amoghavarsha**, who ascended the throne while still young, could not resist Vijayaditya II's strength. **Karkaraju**, a Gujarat feudatory safeguarding the Rashtrakuta kingdom, accepted Vijayaditya's supremacy and gave his daughter Seelamahadevi in marriage to Kalivishnuvardhana, Vijayaditya's son. The Ghurjara-Prathiharas were defeated in Central India, and his remaining rule went on peacefully.
    
*   He is credited with building Siva temples at the 108 places where he fought his battles — installing a Sivalinga and constructing a Siva temple at each battlefield. It is said Bezawada (Vijayawada) got its name because of him.

### Kalivishnuvardhana (847 – 848 A.D.)

Son of Vijayaditya II (also called Vishnuvardhana V). Had four sons: Vijayaditya III, Vikramaditya, Nripakamudu and Yuddhamalla.

### Gunaga Vijayaditya (Vijayaditya III) (849 – 892 A.D.)

The greatest among the Eastern Chalukyas — also called Gunaka Vijayaditya for his many good qualities. He was the ruler who could make the victory-flag of the Chalukyas march "from the Ganges in the North to the Cauvery in the South." Around four decades were spent in wars and crisis.

**Consolidation and administration**

*   To suppress feudatories and establish peace, he appointed brahmin commanders-in-chief of highest loyalty, such as **Pandurangadu**, **Vinayadisarma** and **Rajaditya**.
*   Pandurangadu conquered Boya Kottas, held Nellore and established peace there; a strong fort was built with Kandukoor as the central point, equivalent in importance to Bezawada.
*   Though his mother **Seelamahadevi** was a Rashtrakuta princess, stable peace did not follow between the two dynasties for various reasons. As long as Amoghavarsha lived, the Chalukyas (under Gunaga) remained subordinate to Rashtrakuta authority.

**Military campaigns**

*   Conquered Gangavadi and Nolambavadi in C.E. 870, defeating Ranavikrama, the Gangavadi ruler, at Sivaganga. Rashtrakutas and their allies who supported them fell into trouble at the hands of Gunaga's commander-in-chief. Forts like Achalapuram, Kiranapuram and Chakrakutam got destroyed. The Dahala kingdom (between the Ganga and Narmada rivers), South Kosala and Kalinga kingdoms were subjugated by Chalukyan armies.
*   Achieving great victory and revenge, Rashtrakuta king Krishna had no alternative but to accept Gunaga Vijayaditya's authority. Gunaga took charge of the Pali dhvaja and the Krishna–Yamuna torana, which remained symbols of Eastern Chalukya supreme authority.
*   During his reign, Eastern Chalukyan authority extended from Mahanandi to Pulicat lake, remaining unrivalled in South Indian politics.
*   After the death of Amoghavarsha (C.E. 880), his son **Krishna II** assumed authority but was defeated by Gunaga Vijayaditya; Krishna II had no alternative but to conclude peace with Gunaga and accept his sovereign authority (details recorded in the Dharmavaram, Attili and Paderu inscriptions).
*   The **Sataluru inscription** of Gunaga Vijayaditya records victories against the Pallavas and Pandyas. Defeating the Pallavas and Pandyas, Vijayaditya may have saved a Chola king (possibly Aditya Chola) who had sought Pandurangadu's shelter. Some inscriptions suggest Baddega, the Vemulavada king, was also defeated by him.
*   Making the Rashtrakutas — themselves once conquerors of the entire South India — his feudatories, Gunaga Vijayaditya became the absolute and supreme sovereign of the entire South India. He assumed **titles** such as "tripuramartamaheswara," "parachakrarama" and "ranarangasudraka."

**Decline after his death:** After him, quarrels started in the Vengi Chalukya dynasty over the throne. Taking advantage of these internal disturbances, enemies captured many occupied areas: the Ganga king **Vajrahasta** annexed the Trikalinga kingdom into his own. This brought down the prestige of the Vengi kingdom; the fact that divisions arose within the core strength of the Vengi Chalukyas showed how terrible conditions in the kingdom had become.

### Chalukya Bhima I (892 – 921 A.D.)

His accession was opposed by his uncle **Yuddhamalla I** (his father Gunaga Vijayaditya's brother), who sought help from Rashtrakuta Krishna. His rule did not go on peacefully.

*   Vemulavada king **Baddega**, insulted during Gunaga Vijayaditya's time, came with Rashtrakuta armies and captured Chalukya Bhima in the war fought at Kolleru — possibly when Bhima took shelter in the Kolleru water fort.
*   The **Koravi copper plate inscription (C.E. 935)** informs that, to defeat the Rashtrakuta army, Bhima made **Mahakala**, son of his stepmother, associate with him as Dandanadha (commander-in-chief). Bhima defeated the Rashtrakutas and drove them away.
*   In a fierce battle, **Irimartiganda**, the son of Bhima, killed a Rashtrakuta in the Nidadavolu and Peravanguru battles and sacrificed himself on the battlefield; as a memorial to his heroic son, Bhima made Vedatalur village an agrahara and donated it.
*   Chalukya Bhima installed the Bheemeswaraswamy (temple) at Draksharamam.
*   Around C.E. 900, during his time, the Kanchipura Pallava empire was conquered by the Cholas.
*   His inscriptions record that during his 30-year rule he waged 360 battles.

### Vijayaditya IV / Kollabhiganda (921 A.D.)

Son of Chalukya Bhima I; ruled for only six months in C.E. 921. When **Vajrahasta III** of the Kalinga Ganga dynasty rebelled, the **Viraja battle** was fought against him, in which Vijayaditya IV was defeated and, it appears, died.

### Ammaraju I (921 – 927 A.D.)

Ascended after Vijayaditya IV. It is said Rajamahendrapuram was constructed during his reign and became the Chalukyan capital — as Vengi, being in a flat plain, was easily subjected to enemy attacks, Ammaraju established his capital on the northern coast of the Godavari, bearing the title "rajamahendra."

**Wars of succession:** After Ammaraju's death, succession wars started among the brothers of Gunaga Vijayaditya — Vikramaditya and Yuddhamalla. Up to Ammaraju I, only the descendants of Vikramaditya had ascended the Vengi throne, but Yuddhamalla's line refused to tolerate this and declared war. **Talaraju** (C.E. 927), son of Yuddhamalla I, and then his son **Yuddhamalla II** (C.E. 928–934), occupied the kingdom. Yuddhamalla II is said to have shifted his capital to Bezawada out of insecurity, built a Kartikeya temple there, and issued the famous **Bezawada stone inscription (C.E. 930)**.

### Chalukya Bhima II (934 – 945 A.D.)

Half-brother of Ammaraju I; drove away Yuddhamalla II and occupied the throne. He killed his competitors Tatabikki, Rajamarthanda, Lovabikki, Ayyapa and others who had occupied the throne. He could to some extent limit Rashtrakuta influence in Vengi politics. His wife Ankidevi, daughter of the Kalinga king, may have provided him Rashtrakuta-side help. During his time, the rebellion of the feudatories (Vemulavada Chalukyas) within the Rashtrakuta kingdom against Govinda IV worked to his advantage. He had two sons — Ammaraju II and Danarnava.

### Ammaraju II (945 – 970 A.D.)

Ruled Vengi for 25 years, though dethroned twice. His mother was Lokamahadevi.

*   After his coronation, the grandsons of Yuddhamalla I — **Badaparaju** (C.E. 945) and **Talapa II** — drove him away and occupied the kingdom for some time.
*   Rashtrakuta **Krishna III** then sent an army against Ammaraju; Ammaraju's kingdom was in turn occupied by Krishna III. After Krishna III turned back, Ammaraju returned to Vengi, occupied the kingdom, and reigned up to C.E. 970.
*   He gave donation at Bezawada to a Saiva temple called "samastabhuvanasraya," built by Narendramrigaraju. During his time, the Kalamukha sect developed.
*   At the end, in C.E. 970, his brother **Danarnava** raided him; first defeated, Danarnava sought the help of the Mudigonda Chalukyas and, along with Rashtrakuta Krishna III, killed Ammaraju II and ascended the Vengi throne.

### Danarnava (970 – 973 A.D.)

His mother, Urjapaya, was a princess from Kalinga. Though Krishna III had helped him gain the throne, Danarnava was able to conquer Southern Andhra, which had been lost by the Vengi Chalukyas. Taking advantage of the decline of Rashtrakuta power, he invaded Renadu in C.E. 972, took Velanadu, Konidesa and Pottapinadu under his control, and gifted away Pottapinadu to the Mudigonda Chalukyas who had helped him — thereby gaining rule over 300 villages.

While Danarnava was ruling ably, **Jatachoda Bhima**, a relative of Ammaraju II, attacked him, killed him, and declared himself king.

### Jatachoda Bhima (973 – 999 A.D.)

With his reign, Vengi political history entered its **third stage**. He dashed into Vengi politics; the inscription at the Kailasanatha temple gives information about him. He ruled with **Peddakallu** (Kurnool district) as his capital. Jatachoda was his father, and Vallabhiganda (daughter of Vijayaditya, granddaughter of Chalukya Bhima I, of the Chola dynasty) his mother.

*   The killing of Ammaraju II and Danarnava's seizure of the Vengi kingdom angered Jatachoda Bhima, who attacked Vengi, killed Danarnava, and occupied it. He is not mentioned in Vengi Chalukyan inscriptions.
*   Danarnava's sons, **Saktivarma and Vimaladitya**, fled to Kalinga and, with the help of Ganga Kamarnava, invaded Vengi; to confront them Jatachoda Bhima fought unending battles on all sides and defeated the Kalinga forces.
*   As his authority strengthened in Vengi and Kalinga, Saktivarma and Vimaladitya, not knowing what to do, ran away to the Chola kingdom for shelter. Chola king **Rajaraja Chola** (C.E. 985–1013) then ruled, and clashes had begun between the Cholas and the Western Chalukyas of Karnataka for South Indian supremacy.
*   Realizing that resisting Western Chalukya aggression required Chola predominance in Vengi, Rajaraja strengthened political ties by giving his daughter Kundavva in marriage to Vimaladitya; with Chola help, Saktivarma re-entered Vengi and warred with Jatachoda Bhima, and these wars are recorded in the Prabhuparru and Penneru inscriptions.
*   Jatachoda Bhima drove away Saktivarma and the Chola army up to Kanchipuram, but died near Kanchipuram itself in the battle fought there, in C.E. 999. Vengi and Kalinga then came under Saktivarma's control.

### Saktivarma (1000 – 1011 A.D.)

Came to the throne in C.E. 1000 after defeating Jatachoda Bhima; Vengi and Kalinga came under his control. His brother **Vimaladitya** (C.E. 1011–1018) succeeded him.

*   Both brothers were anxious to bring Vengi fully under their own control, and Chalukyan prestige began to decline as the balance of power in South Indian politics was disrupted by growing Chola dominance in Vengi (unacceptable to the Western Chalukyas).
*   Clashes began between Chola Rajaraja (C.E. 985–1013) and the Western Chalukya ruler; Vengi became the centre for these clashes. Law and order declined completely, exposing the weakness of the Vengi Chalukyas and causing much political damage to Vengi.
*   Saktivarma bore the title "**Chalukya Chandrudu**"; coins with this title have been found on the Arakan coast, indicating traders of the day travelled to eastern islands for trade.

### Vimaladitya (1011 – 1018 A.D.)

Became king after Saktivarma's death; his coronation took place in May, 1011 A.D., with titles "rajamarthanda" and "mummidibhima." Details of his eight-year rule are sparse. Some historians hold that Karnataka forces attacked Vengi during his time; unable to resist, he fled to Cholamandalam and returned with his uncle's support to regain the kingdom.

Though a Saiva in the beginning, he later accepted **Jainism**; Desiganacharya, "trikalayogi" and "siddhantadeva" were his gurus at the time of his initiation into Jainism. He built a cave temple called Ramakonda at Ramathirtham (Visakhapatnam mandalam).

### Rajaraja Narendra (1019 – 1061 A.D.)

Vimaladitya had two wives: **Kundavva**, daughter of Chola emperor Rajaraja, and **Melima**, princess of the Telugu Choda dynasty. Kundavva gave birth to **Rajaraja Narendra**; Melima gave birth to **Vijayaditya**.

**Succession dispute and Chola intervention**

*   After Vimaladitya's death, his son Rajaraja Narendra was to assume kingship, but as the kingdom did not come under his control, his coronation was held only after four years.
*   His step-brother **Vijayaditya** disliked Rajaraja Narendra's accession and allied with **Jayasimha II** (the Karnataka Chalukya emperor) and **Madhukamarnava** (the Kalinga Ganga king), occupying Vengi.
*   Rajaraja Narendra, unable to oppose them, went to Cholamandalam as his ancestors had done and sought Chola help. By then his maternal grandfather Rajaraja Chola had died, and his uncle, **Rajendrachola**, was ruling the empire. Feeling pity for his nephew's distress and troubled by Vengi's fall into other hands, emperor **Rajendra Chola** invaded and defeated Vijayaditya and his allies, driving them from Vengi and celebrating Rajaraja Narendra's coronation on **16th August, C.E. 1022**.
*   Rajendra Chola's daughter, Ammangadevi, was Rajaraja Narendra's wife.

**Ongoing conflict**

*   Many matters relating to his reign are unclear, but when the Cholas helped him, the Western Chalukyas and Kalinga (who did not tolerate Chola presence in Vengi) helped Vijayaditya instead.
*   With Western Chalukya king **Aahavamalla Someswara** on one side and **Rajadhiraja** (who became the Chola ruler) on the other, mutual clashes intensified. Someswara conquered Vengi and Kalinga; his feudatories, such as Sobhanarasu, assumed the title "Vengipuravareswara."
*   Rajadhiraja made great, sustained efforts over more than ten years — more than ten battles were fought to destroy Chalukyan domination at Vengi. In the **Dharanikota battle**, Western Chalukya commanders-in-chief Gangadhara and Gandapayya were killed; Chola armies occupied territory up to Kollipaka.
*   Details of the Chola–Western Chalukya wars in this period are not fully clear. When Rajadhiraja died in the **Kopparam war (C.E. 1053)**, this meant the loss of Chola protection for Rajaraja Narendra — leaving no option except to accept the supremacy of Ahavamalla Someswara.

**Cultural patronage:** Just as his contemporary Bhojamaharaja patronised Sanskrit poets, Rajaraja Narendra patronised Telugu poets and won fame; his contribution to Telugu language was more remarkable even than Bhoja's contribution to Sanskrit. **Nannaya**, the poet titled "sabdasasana," adorned his court. The first two-and-a-half parvas of the _Andhra Mahabharata_ were written by Nannaya, assisted by **Narayanabhattu**.

### Rajendra (Kulottunga Chola) and the End of Vengi Chalukyas (to 1075 A.D.)

After Rajaraja Narendra's death, his son **Rajendra** was to ascend the throne, but the details of the events at this time are unclear. His uncle (father's step-brother) **Vijayaditya** (C.E. 1061–1075) occupied the throne, preventing Rajendra's accession.

*   Rajendra's uncle (mother's brother), **Rajendra Chola II**, tried to drive Vijayaditya VII from Vengi and restore Rajendra to his father's kingdom. After Rajendra Chola II, **Virarajendra** raided several times and, at last in C.E. 1067, conquered Vengi, Kalinga and Chakrakuta.
*   It is not clear why Rajendra was not given his father's kingdom; instead his uncle-rival Vijayaditya was preferred and kept in Chakrakuta mandal. Afterward, in a short period when Virarajendra died, Rajendra came from Chakrakutam to Vengi, defeated Vijayaditya, and — in order to join Vengi to the Chola empire — came to war with Vijayaditya; but the latter received help from **Rajraja Devendra Varma**, the Eastern Ganga king, and **Yasahkarnadeva**, the Chedi king, and as a result, Rajendra's army was defeated.
*   Rajendra, in order to defeat Vijayaditya, made a plan of marrying his daughter, Rajasundari, to Devendravarma. As **Vijayaditya died in C.E. 1075**, the Vengi Chalukya dynasty came to an end. Rajendra, who had ascended the Chola throne with the title **Kulottunga Chola**, finally joined Vengi into the Chola empire.

### Chola – Western Chalukya Relations in Vengi

Chola Rajaraja, keeping the interest of his empire in view and aiming to bring Vengi under his rule, gave shelter to Saktivarma and Vimaladitya. He gave Vimaladitya his daughter Kundavva in marriage, and made Saktivarma the king of Vengi — turning the Vengi kingdom into a Chola-protected kingdom.

Chola influence in Vengi became an eyesore to the Kalyani Chalukyas, who had their eye on sovereign authority over South India. With Vengi remaining the battleground between the Chola and Kalyani Chalukyas, many battles took place. Eastern Chalukya king Saktivarma turned back a Kalyani Chalukya attack with Chola help; his brother Vimaladitya married Chola princess Kundavva, and also Melima, daughter of Jatachoda Bhima.

The coronation of Rajaraja Narendra was delayed due to the conflicting efforts of the Kalinga king Madhukamarnava (desiring to free himself from Vengi Chalukya hegemony), the Kalyani Chalukya king Jayasimha (aiming to end Chola dominance), and — as a climax — Vijayaditya VII planning to occupy the Vengi throne with the help of both these rulers. Vijayaditya's efforts to occupy Vengi with Chola help were foiled by Rajara Narendra.

As Jayasimha, the Kalyani Chalukya king, died, his son **Ahavamalla Someswara** ascended the throne. Later, when Rajendra Chola died, **Rajadhiraja** came to the Chola throne. During the time of these two rulers, Chalukya–Chola conflict reached a high pitch, and Vengi witnessed chaos. Ahavamalla foiled Chola efforts and established Kalyani Chalukyan dominance at Vengi.

With the death of Ahavamalla (C.E. 1068), internal struggle started among his sons. Afterward, Virarajendra died within two years, and in a few weeks his son Adhirajendra also died. Eastern Chalukyan king Rajendra occupied Gangaikonda Cholapuram and, with the name Kulottunga Chola, ascended the throne. After the death of **Vijayaditya VII (C.E. 1075)**, Vengi finally became joined to the Chola empire.

Vemulavada Chalukyas were feudatories of the Rashtrakutas, ruling the north-western Telangana region with **Vemulavada** (Karimnagar district) as their capital. As feudatories of the Rashtrakutas, they ruled from C.E. 750 to 975 — around 225 years. Their rule, which started with the kindness of the Rashtrakutas, also ended with the Rashtrakutas.

**Sources:** Six stone inscriptions and two copper-plate inscriptions are the main sources for their history — the Kuruvagattu stone inscription (Mahaboobnagar), the Karimnagar inscription (C.E. 946), and the Vemulavada stone inscriptions issued by Arikesari II. The Chennur stone inscription (C.E. 941) of Arikesari II records that Yuddhamalla I was opposed by the Mudigonda Chalukya king, Vijayaditya; when the latter invaded him, he sought the help of Vemulavada king Arikesari II, who not only sheltered Vijayaditya but also made him administrator of the Chennur region. The Kurkyala inscriptions (C.E. 940) of Jinavallabha and the stone inscriptions in the Karimnagar museum reveal the genealogy of the Vemulavada Chalukyas; the Kollipara copper-plate inscription of Arikesari I and the Parbhani copper plate (C.E. 966) of Arikesari III help reconstruct their history. Literary works — **Vikramarjuna Vijayam** by Pampa, and **Yasastilaka Champukavyam** by the Jain scholar Somadevasuri (also useful for religious and social conditions and political details) — are additional sources. Hindu and Jain temples built at Repaka, Korutla and Bommalagutta serve as archaeological sources. Nelatoori Venkataramanaiah undertook integrated research on the Vemulavada kings and, after gathering the available information, wrote works in English and Telugu.

### Early Rulers

As per their inscriptions, the founder of the dynasty was **Satyasraya Ranavikrama (C.E. 650–675)**. His sons **Prithvipathi (C.E. 675–700)** and **Maharaju (C.E. 700–725)**, and the latter's son **Prithvivikrama (C.E. 725–750)**, all ruled, but details of their reigns, where they ruled, and the extent of the kingdom are not clearly known.

### Vinayaditya Yuddhamalla (750 – 775 A.D.)

Founder of the Vemulavada Chalukyan kingdom (as an established, better-documented line). The political history of the first four rulers of this branch, up to Vinayaditya Yuddhamalla, is not clear. He is described as a great conqueror. Historians opine he was the son of Dharasraya Jayasimhavarma; some argue he was the brother of Pulakesi only.

*   He joined as commander-in-chief of **Dantidurga**, founder of the Rashtrakuta empire, and participated in his wars.
*   He is said to have ruled **Sapadalaksha** (a kingdom of one lakh twenty-five thousand villages) — no one else would have ruled such a kingdom — had all his elephants bathed in an oil tank at Podana, conquered the impregnable Chitrakuta fort, and won Dantidurga's appreciation.
*   Impressed by his services, Dantidurga appointed him feudatory for the areas of Bodhan (Nizamabad) and Karimnagar; he ruled with **Bodhan** as his capital.
*   Pampa's _Vikramarjuna Vijayam_ mentions he had elephant forces in greater numbers, and that he conquered Turkish, Yavana, Barbara, Kashmira, Kamboja, Magadha, Kalinga, Ganga, Pallava, Pandya and Kerala areas. The Kollipara copper-plate inscriptions state that the rulers of these kingdoms worshipped at his feet.

### Arikesari I (775 – 800 A.D.)

Assumed authority after his father Vinayaditya Yuddhamalla's death. He was a feudatory of Rashtrakuta **Dhruva** (C.E. 780–793).

*   In the war of succession between Dhruva and his brother Govinda II, Arikesari I supported Dhruva; the Kollipara copper-plate inscription informs that when Eastern Chalukya ruler Vishnuvardhana IV helped Govinda, the wars fought as a reaction to this were led by Arikesari I, and in these wars, Vishnuvardhana gave his daughter Seelamahadevi in marriage to Rashtrakuta Dhruva.
    
*   As a mark of victory, the Kuruvagattu inscription records that Dhruva gifted Arikesari I the areas of Nagarkurnool in Mahaboobnagar district and Ramadugu in Nalgonda district. With this eastward extension, the capital shifted from Bodhan to **Vemulavada**.
    
*   Arikesari I made an educational donation of Belmoga village to Mugdhasivacharya, disciple of Kalamukha Saivacharya Sadyasivacharya. His kingdom extended to the regions of Nalgonda, Karimnagar and Mahaboobnagar.
    
*   The Kollipara inscription records he was a great scholar with remarkable prowess in Gajatantra, archery and Ayurveda, and held titles such as "samastalokasraya," "tribhuvanamalla," "rajatrinetra" and "sahasrarayadi."
    
*   After Arikesari I, his sons in order — **Narasimha I (C.E. 800–825)** and the latter's son **Yuddhamalla II (C.E. 825–850)** — ruled. During their fifty-year rule, no victories or developments of note occurred.

### Baddega (850 – 895 A.D.)

Son of Yuddhamalla II. Held the title "**soladaganda**," meaning "a warrior who knew no defeat" — earned through victory in **forty-two battles**.

*   The Parbhani inscription (C.E. 966) records he invaded Vengi, defeated Chalukya Bhima, and took him into custody "just like catching a crocodile in a pond."
*   Eastern Chalukyan inscriptions also state that Baddega defeated Gunaga Vijayaditya. After Gunaga's death, in the revengeful war waged by Rashtrakuta **Krishna II**, Baddega played a leading role.
*   But Kusumayudha, of the Mudigonda Chalukya dynasty, defeated Baddega, drove him away, got Chalukya Bhima released from captivity, and enabled him to ascend the throne — so despite his title "soladaganda," Baddega could not avoid this defeat.
    
*   He built a temple in his own name at Vemulavada, known as the Baddegeswara temple — now famous as the Vemulavada **Bheemeswara temple**.
*   After Baddega, his son **Yuddhamalla III** ruled from C.E. 895 to 915, though details of his reign are not available. After him, his son **Narasimha II (C.E. 915–930)** brought successes back to the dynasty.

### Narasimha II (915 – 930 A.D.)

Came to the throne in C.E. 915 as successor to Yuddhamalla III. A warrior of great strength who won many battles; through a military expedition up to the Ganges river, he secured a place of importance in the history of the age.

*   He was the feudatory of Rashtrakuta **Indra III** (C.E. 915–922), participating in Indra III's northern Indian military expedition. On Indra III's orders, he invaded the northern region, conquered Lata and Saptamalava, and collected tribute. He later invaded Kanyakubjam, defeated **Mahipala** (C.E. 912–944), the Gurjara Prathihara ruler, and drove him away — an attack which, made with Indra III's help, dealt a serious blow to the Prathihara kingdom from which it did not recover.
*   The **Vemulavada inscription** records that as Mahipala fled, Narasimha II's chasing horses bathed in the Ganga river; on the return march, as a mark of victory, he erected a victory pillar at Kalapriyam (opined by Altekar to be on the coast of the Yamuna river).
*   Narasimha II and Indra III were friends, relatives and contemporaries — the wife of Narasimha II happened to be the sister of Indra III; her name was **Jakavva**, and she became the mother of **Arikesari II**. Appreciating Narasimha II's victories, Indra III is thought to have married his sister to him.
*   During his time, Jaina "choumukhas" (four-faced Jain images) were carved at Vemulavada. His military abilities and leadership were responsible for his extraordinary rise — "an ordinary leader with limited authority could never dream about such elevation."

### Arikesari II (930 – 955 A.D.)

Among the Vemulavada Chalukya rulers, Arikesari II earned the most name — admired as a scholar, warrior, good ruler, great organiser and patron of poets.

**Political role**

*   War of succession erupted in the Rashtrakuta kingdom during his time: when **Amoghavarsha II** (son of Indra III) ascended the throne, he was dethroned by his younger brother **Govinda IV**, who led a life without peace due to his cruelty and immoral behaviour, causing many enemies to spring up.
*   His uncle Baddega and Krishna (son of Baddega) prepared plans for dethroning Govinda IV; parallel wars of succession also took place in Vengi after Chalukya Bhima I.
*   **Vijayaditya** of Mudigonda Chalukya dynasty joined Arikesari II and fought the Rashtrakutas. Under these circumstances, Baddega was invited by Arikesari II to Vemulavada; he was declared Rashtrakuta emperor, defeated Govinda IV's armies in many battles and drove him away, and Baddega (under the name **Amoghavarsha III**) was installed on the Rashtrakuta throne.

**Patronage and achievements**

*   Under his patronage, the **first great work in Kannada literature, Pampa's "Vikramarjuna Vijayam,"** was written during his rule. **Aditya Griham** was built at Vemulavada.
*   He married **Revakanirmadi**, daughter of Indra III and Lokambika, another Rashtrakuta princess.
*   His titles: pambaramkusa, ammaanagandhavarana, udattanarayana, gunanidhi, gunarnava, saranagata, vajrapanjara, priyagala, tribhuvanamalla, samantachudamani.
*   Of his four surviving inscriptions, the **Vemulavada inscription** (in Sanskrit) is the most important, giving the genealogy of the Vemulavada Chalukyas from Vinayaditya Yuddhamalla to Arikesari II. This same inscription states that **Peddanaryudu**, his war minister, built Adityalaya at Vemulavada, coming to the temple on Sankranti day to donate 100 nivaratnas of land.
*   **Pampa** was his court poet, and in _Vikramarjuna Vijayam_ compared Arikesari II to Arjuna. Delighted with the work, Arikesari II gave Pampa Dharmapuri (Jagityal Taluka) as an agrahara.
*   The Baddega inscription found at Chennur (Adilabad district, C.E. 941) states his kingdom extended from Bodhan to Chennur.
*   He had two sons: **Vegaraju** (born to Revakanirmadi), the eldest, and **Baddega II** (born to Lokambika).

### Vegaraju (955 – 960 A.D.)

Eldest son of Arikesari II, assumed royal authority — also a feudatory of Krishna III. He ruled the kingdom with **Gangadhara** town as his capital; this was located at Yelpadi (Chittoor district). Somadevasuri, in his chempukavya, states he completed writing his work in Saka era 881 (C.E. 959) during Vegaraju's time (during the time of Arikesari II, per the source).

### Baddega II / Bhadradeva (960 – 965 A.D.)

As Vegaraju had no children, his younger brother Baddega II (Bhadradeva) came to the throne. He issued an inscription at Vemulavada, and, for the sake of Somadevasuri, built a Jaina monastery of Gauda Sangha named **subhadamajenalaya**. During his time, Bommala gattu developed into a great Jaina centre.

### Arikesari III (965 – 973 A.D.) — Last of the Vemulavada Chalukyas

Son of Baddega II; the **last king of the Vemulavada Chalukya dynasty**. He issued the Parbhani copper-plate inscription (966 A.D.) and the Karimnagar copper-plate inscription (946 A.D.). Vemulavada was his capital.

*   He granted Repaka village (in present-day Sircilla taluka) to "subhadamajenalayam," which had been built by his father for Somadevasuri's sake. The Repaka inscription (968 A.D.) confirms a Jaina temple was built there and granted land.
*   His titles: pambaramkusa, vidyadhara, vikramarjuna, samantachudamani.

**End of the dynasty:** In **973 A.D., he destroyed the Rashtrakuta dynasty and established the Kalyani Chalukya kingdom with Tailapa II as king.** Along with the Rashtrakutas, Vemulavada Chalukya rule also came to an end in 973 A.D.

Vemulavada Chalukyas ruled Karimnagar and Nizamabad districts as though it was a golden age; many Hindu and Jain temples were built in these areas, and the Rajarajeswara and Baddigeswara (Bhimeswara) temples became famous. Their role in Telangana history was remarkable.

* * *

Mudigonda Chalukyas ruled over **Manchikondanadu in Koraviseema** (present Telangana), with **Mudigonda** (Khammam district) as their capital. The Khammam and Warangal areas came to be known as "Koraviseema" — the eastern part of which was called Manchikondanadu. Like the Vemulavada Chalukya kingdom, the Mudigonda kingdom lay on the borders of the Vengi and Malkhed empires and controlled all the routes entering Vengi. Mudigonda Chalukyas guarded the north-western borders of the Vengi Chalukyas and carried on their rule as trusted feudatories of the Vemulavada Chalukyas and their neighbours — the Eastern Chalukyas and Rashtrakutas.

**Sources:** The Koravi copper-plate inscription (C.E. 935) and the Mogalcheruvu inscription cover the period up to the Eastern Chalukyan age; for later history, the Viriyalavari Gudoor inscription (C.E. 1124) and the Krivvaka inscription of Kusumayudha are the main sources. As these inscriptions have no dates and their information is inadequate, there was limited opportunity to know their full history.

### Ranamardhudu — Founder

Founder of the Mudigonda Chalukyan dynasty, possibly belonging to the Western Chalukyan family line. He acquired Koravi mandalam with the help of the Eastern Chalukyas and ruled from Mudigonda.

### Kusumayudhudu / Kusumayudha I (C.E. 870 – 895)

Son of Ranamardhudu (per the Koravi inscription). He was contemporary with Gunaga Vijayaditya and Chalukya Bhima, and played a leading role in the Vengi Chalukya–Rashtrakuta conflict of his time.

*   After the death of Gunaga Vijayaditya, Rashtrakuta Krishna II, in a revengeful attitude, first occupied the Koravi region and then led an expedition against the Vengi Chalukyas; in response, Kusumayudha attacked the Rashtrakutas, freed Chalukya Bhima from Krishna II's captivity, installed him on the throne, drove the Rashtrakutas from Koraviseema, and skilfully got the empire protected, and with the empire being handed back to Chalukya Bhima, Kusumayudha earned respect in several ways.
    

### Gonagaiah (895 – 910 A.D.)

Kusumayudha had two sons, Gonagaiah and Niravadya; out of regard for Gunaga Vijayaditya, one son was named "Gonagaiah" (the short form of Gunaga Vijayaditya). Gonagaiah was also called Karigonaga ("black Gonaga"). After Kusumayudha, Gonagaiah ascended the throne. Because of internal conflicts that arose in Vengi after Chalukya Bhima, Gonagaiah lost the affection of the Vengi Chalukyas.

Taking advantage of these developments, his brother Niravadya (C.E. 910–935) removed Gonagaiah and himself ascended the Mudigonda Chalukyan throne, as recorded by the Koravi inscription; having lost the kingdom, Gonagaiah sought the help of Arikesari II (C.E. 930–955), and with his help, dethroned Niravadya and got the Mudigonda kingdom back. In the later period, only the descendants of Gonagaiah ruled over the Mudigonda kingdom.

### The Emergence of the Kakatiyas and Mudigonda–Kakatiya Conflict

In this period, the **Kakatiya kingdom emerged**. Perhaps with the idea of keeping the Mudigonda Chalukyas in check, Rashtrakuta king Krishna II appointed his commander-in-chief **Yeriya** as administrator over **Kurravadi** (only part of the Koravi kingdom). Gundaya, the father of Yeriya, was a Rashtrakuta, referred to in the Machilipatnam inscription of Chalukya Bhima as Dandeva Gundana. Perhaps Yeriya made **Orugallu (present Warangal)** his capital — with this, the Kakatiya dynasty was installed.

*   From this point, **Kakatiya–Mudigonda Chalukya conflict** began; the incidents of the first stage are not clearly known, but because of the rise of the Kakatiyas, the Chalukyas appear to have been forced temporarily to leave Koravi.
*   Yeriya's son was **Betiya**, and Betiya's son was **Kakartiya Gundana**. It appears Betiya was driven away and the Mudigonda Chalukyas reoccupied Koraviseema. But, during their period, in the conflict that occurred for the Chalukyan throne (Vengi), **Danarnava** killed his younger brother Ammarajamahendra and ascended the Vengi throne. For helping in this, Danarnava made Kakartya Gundana ruler of **Natavadi**, and tried to send the Mudigonda Chalukyas to the Renati region.
*   In the meantime, political conditions changed in both the Vengi and Rashtrakuta kingdoms: in Vengi, Danarnava was removed by **Jatachoda Bhima**; and in the Rashtrakuta kingdom, **Tailapa II** (Kalyani Chalukyas) removed the Rashtrakuta dynasty. In this situation, Kakartya Gundana invaded Koraviseema, defeated the Mudigonda Chalukyas, and reoccupied **Kurravadi kingdom**, which had been lost by his father Betiya.
*   The Mudigonda Chalukyas, having lost their kingdom, sought Tailapa II's help. As both were Chalukyan families, and the Kakatiyas had been their enemy commanders-in-chief, Tailapa II decided to remove the Kakatiyas and restore Koraviseema to the Mudigonda Chalukyas. Tailapa II entrusted this task to his commander, **Viriyala Yerrabhupati**, who defeated Kakartya Gundana, killed him, and — as stated in the Gudoor inscription (C.E. 1124) — installed **Bottu Betadu** as king in Koraviseema. According to the Krivvaka inscription, **Bottu Bethadu (C.E. 1125–50)**, installed by Yerrabhupati, is learnt to be of Mudigonda Chalukya dynasty. Either way, based on these two inscriptions, Bottu Bethadu of the Mudigonda Chalukya dynasty again became king of Koraviseema.

**Later succession:** Due to Kakartya Gundana's death, his son **Garuda Betaraju**, being a minor, lost the kingdom and became helpless. Seeing the minor child, **Kamasani**, wife of Yerrabhupati, took pity on him, sought Tailapa's help, and could get the kingdom back to Betaraju. Tailapa gave the **Hanumakonda** area to Garuda Betaraju. As a result of this arrangement, the Kakatiyas in Warangal and the Mudigonda Chalukyas in Koraviseema got stabilised, and both became feudatories of Tailapa II.

*   The **Palampeta inscription** informs that **Kakati Rudra** invaded the Mudigonda Chalukyas (feudatories of the Kalyani Chalukyas) and drove them away. In the later period, after the death of **Rudradeva**, the Mudigonda Chalukyas reoccupied Koraviseema.

### Kusumayudha VI (1150 – 1175 A.D.) — Last of the Mudigonda Chalukyas

Learnt from the Krivvaka inscription to be the **last ruler among the Mudigonda Chalukyas**. During the time of his younger brother, **Nagatiraju (C.E. 1175–1200)**, **Ganapatideva** (Kakatiya kingdom) invaded the Mudigonda Chalukyan kingdom, defeated him and drove him away.

With this, the Mudigonda Chalukyan kingdom became part of the Kakatiya empire; it is learnt that the last Mudigonda Chalukyas, having lost the kingdom, went to Vengi, stayed there for some time, and died — and with their death, the Mudigonda Chalukya dynasty, it is learnt, has ended.
