Among the great dynasties that ruled South India and exercised influence over Andhradesa, the Kalyani Chalukyas deserve mention. Though the language of their inscriptions is Kannada and the area they mostly ruled was Karnataka, the works _Prabhanda Chintamani_ and _Rasamalaprabandham_, written by **Meruthunga Charyulu**, state that they belong to Telangana. Kalyani Chalukyas are also called **Western Chalukyas**, and belong to the Badami Chalukya dynastic line.

The Rashtrakuta empire, established after overthrowing the Badami Chalukya dynasty, continued for two and a half centuries and suffered decline at the hands of **Tailapa II**, who belonged to the Kalyani Chalukyan dynasty. The first capital of the Kalyani Chalukyas was **Manyakheta**; later they made **Kalyani** their capital and ruled from there for around 200 years. Their rule was established by Tailapa II.

### Tailapa II (973 – 997 A.D.)

By 957 A.D. he was a feudatory of the Rashtrakutas, belonging to the dynasty of **Satyasraya Bhimarasu**, who ruled the Hanumakonda area as a Rashtrakuta feudatory. He was the son of Vikramaditya IV and Bontadevi. As Bontadevi was a Chedi princess, Tailapa may have secured Chedi help in overthrowing the Rashtrakutas. Some opine he belonged to the dynasty of Bhimarasu, uncle (father's brother) of the last Badami Chalukya ruler Keertivarma II — from the title "mahamandaleswara" of Tailapa II, it appears he was a feudatory of the Rashtrakutas.

*   By defeating **Karka II**, the last Rashtrakuta king, in **C.E. 973**, the sovereignty of the Kalyani Chalukyas was established. He had no titles until C.E. 957; by C.E. 965, he assumed the titles "mahasamantadhipa," "chalukyarama," "satyasrayakula tilaka," "ahavamalla," "prithvi vallabha."
*   Chola emperor Rajaraja was his contemporary. With Hanumakonda as capital and ruling over Western Telangana as the ancestral area — and as a feudatory under the Rashtrakutas, as known from inscriptions — the works _Prabhanda Chintamani_ and _Rasamala Prabhandam_ claim he was the head of Telangana. **Jakavva**, wife of Tailapa II, was the daughter of Karka II, the Rashtrakuta king.

**Wars**

*   In the north, **Munjaraja**, the Paramara king, was his enemy and invaded him sixteen times as a rival. Once Tailapa imprisoned Munjaraja, who escaped and fled; the last time, in C.E. 995, when Munjaraju crossed the Godavari, **Yadava Bhillama**, Tailapa's feudatory, attacked and killed him in battle. Though Tailapa had imprisoned Munjaraja earlier, Mrunalavati, the widowed sister of Tailapa, loved Munjaraja and helped him escape; he was caught and killed, "as 'prabhanda chintamani' informs in a terrible manner."
*   In the south, Tailapa II could not escape trouble from the Cholas — described in inscriptions as a "devastating fire" in respect of the Cholas, suggesting he fought several battles with them; enmity developed between Tailapa and the Cholas. When Rajaraja Chola occupied Mysore and began acting aggressively, **Tailapa in C.E. 992 defeated them and took away their elephant force as a gift.** He also defeated the Paramaras and Cholas, and conquered Lata, Ghurjara and Pallikota areas; the Banavasi area was joined to his kingdom.
*   **Badaparaja**, of the Chalukya dynasty, was his commander-in-chief. **Ranna**, one of the "kaviratnatrayam" poets in Kannada literature, flourished in Tailapa's court.

### Satyasraya (997 – 1008 A.D.)

Eldest son of Tailapa II; bore the titles "irivabendaga" and "akalamka charita." He ascended the Kalyani Chalukya throne in 997 A.D. As crown prince, remaining as his father's right hand, he helped him in many battles — his title "irivabendaga" suggests that, in battle, he used to pierce himself toward the enemy army.

*   During his reign, enmity with the Cholas became serious: Satyasraya did not tolerate the Cholas coming closer to Vengi, giving protection to **Saktivarma and Vimaladitya**, the two sons of Danarnava. Chola Rajaraja invaded Karnataka and conquered Gangavadi and Nolambavadi; as a result, his entire time was spent fighting continuous wars against the Cholas.
*   His daughter Pampadevi was given in marriage to Pallava king Irivanolambadhi. To protect Vengi from Chalukyan armies, Rajaraja sent one army to Vengi to help Saktivarma, and another under his son Rajendra Chola on an expedition against Rattapadi.
*   The **Mattur inscription (C.E. 1007)** informs that with a huge, fully-armed force stationed near Donapoor, people were butchered without discriminating women, children, the aged and brahmins, and the kingdom was looted. Chola inscriptions record that Banavasi and Kollipaka were conquered; the Chalukyan armies from Vengi were attacked again at Kollipaka by the Chola armies and were defeated — Satyasraya got subjected to some humiliation.
*   **Vimalachandra**, a Jain scholar, was guru to Satyasraya.

### Vikramaditya V (1008 – 1018 A.D.)

As Satyasraya had no sons, and his brother Dasavarna had died earlier, the younger brother's son, Vikramaditya V, assumed royal authority in C.E. 1008 and ruled up to C.E. 1018, with the title "tribhuvanamalla."

*   Though **Nolambhadiraju**, the son-in-law of Satyasraya, accepted his supremacy, **Kundamarasu**, who was looking after Banavasi affairs, opposed him. As Kundamarasu described himself as "death to devour the Cholas," it is assumed he also fought against the Cholas.
*   Vikramaditya V was liberal and made donations; he had a sister named Akkadevi.

### Jayasimha II (1018 – 1042 A.D.)

After Vikramaditya V, his younger brother Ayyana became king but died before coronation could take place; his younger brother **Jayasimha II** ascended the throne. By the time his rule commenced, the kingdom was in difficulties.

*   To avenge the humiliation caused to Munjaraja, Bhojaraja invaded the Chalukyan kingdom and occupied parts of it; inscriptions record that Bhoja conquered Karnataka, Lata and Konkan areas and held victory celebrations. But, contrary to Paramara inscriptions, Chalukyan inscriptions state that Jayasimha defeated the Paramaras and occupied the Northern areas of Kolhapur.
    
*   His commander-in-chief, **Chavanarasu**, also held the title "Konkana dhoomaketa." Around C.E. 1020–24, conflicts between the Chalukya and Paramara dynasties reached an intensive form; Jayasimha personally led an expedition against the Paramara king. Chalukyan inscriptions state Saptamalava was conquered.
    
*   Jayasimha also faced war from the Cholas; Nolambavadi and Bellari areas were subjected to Chola attack, but inscriptions inform that all these areas were reoccupied. **Rajendra Chola defeated Jayasimha in the battle at Maski** and by C.E. 1026, occupied Rattapadi areas. As a result, the Chola war became serious; some say he began construction of the Kalyana fort in C.E. 1028.
*   Jayasimha II had two wives — **Devalamahadevi** and **Suggaladevi** — who together, in C.E. 1029, donated Puligera area to Brahmarasi Pandita, a Pasupathacharya. Though he followed Jain religious principles in the beginning, he accepted **Kalamukha Saivism** due to the encouragement of these queens.
*   His kingdom extended over the districts of Cuddapah and Anantapur in Rayalaseema, and the entire Telangana region. His titles: "jagadekamalla," "trailokamalla," "vikramasimha."

### Someswara I (1042 – 1068 A.D.)

After Jayasimha II, his son Someswara I assumed power in C.E. 1042 and ruled up to C.E. 1068, with the titles "aahavamalla," "rajanarayana" and "trailokamalla." He was the greatest among the Kalyani Chalukyas.

*   **Bilhana**, in his _Vikramankadeva Charita_, mentions that Someswara built the **Kalyani city**, made it his capital and ruled from it. His chief queen, **Mylaladevi**, visited Srisailam in C.E. 1059 and donated gifts to Sureswara, a Jain scholar who was a Kalamukha Saiva guru.
*   Nearly twelve fierce battles were fought with the Cholas even during his reign. By the time he assumed authority, he used to look after the affairs of the Potlakere region.
*   After Someswara I ascended the throne, as Vijayaditya made one more effort to occupy Vengi, his help was sought; thinking Chola authority at Vengi could be removed, his army was sent. With this army, Vijayaditya defeated Rajaraja Narendra, drove him out, and occupied Vengi.
*   His successful expedition went through Vengi, Kalinga, Panchala, Magadha, Malwa and Kerala kingdoms. Wars with Paramara rulers that had begun earlier continued during his time; the rulers of Konkan, Sevuna and Vindhya regions supported the Paramaras. His commander-in-chief **Nagavarma** participated in many wars, fought ably and achieved victories.
*   **Kakatiyas came into prominence during the time of Someswara I.** In the expedition Someswara made on Konkan and Chakrakuta, **Prolaraju I** of the Kakatiya dynasty participated, and appreciating his services, was given control over Hanumakonda and honoured. Prola's son, **Betaraju**, along with Someswara, participated in the wars fought with the Paramaras and Cholas.
*   Because of Rajaraja's statecraft, Chola influence in Vengi politics increased, leading to battles with the Western Chalukyas. After Rajaraja Narendra (C.E. 1022–61) came to the Vengi throne, Chola dominance in Vengi increased; conditions worsened, and internal conflicts took the stage. Vijayaditya, the half-brother of Rajaraja Narendra training to capture kingship, provided an opportunity for Western Chalukya entry into Vengi politics.

**Continued conflict and death**

*   Someswara I fought many battles with the Cholas while helping Vijayaditya, who resisted Rajarajanarendra and carried on his rule with Chola help and per Rajarajanarendra's whims. The **Kalidindi inscription of Rajaraja Narendra** informs that three leading Chola commanders-in-chief were killed at the hands of Western Chalukyan armies. Even during Someswara's time, battles were fought fiercely; his commanders-in-chief Gandapaiah and Gangadhara got killed in war at the hands of the Cholas, and Vijayaditya, Vikramaditya, Madhusudana, Ganapati and Angamaiah (commander-in-chief) all had to flee. With the Cholas' rise, the Western Chalukyas suffered huge losses and several cities were destroyed.
*   In the **Kopparam battle of C.E. 1053–54**, the Western Chalukyas killed Chola **Rajadhiraja**; Rajaraja Narendra, receiving no help from the Cholas under these circumstances, had no alternative except to accept the sovereignty of the Western Chalukyas.
*   Someswara, who fought many battles — the Kanchi invasion (C.E. 1049), the Kopparam war (C.E. 1053–54), a raid on Vengi (C.E. 1061), and the Mudakkara battle (C.E. 1062) — had parts of his kingdom apportioned: his wife Mylaladevi was appointed supervisor over Banavasi region, son **Someswara II** was appointed over Belvala and Puligere areas, and another son **Vikramaditya VI** was appointed supervisor over Gangavadi region.
*   The life of Someswara, who achieved many victories, ended tragically. In his last days, he was defeated in two wars fought at Kudali Sangamam. He asked the Cholas to come for battle the next day, but when the Chola armies arrived at the appointed time, Someswara did not come to the field. As he failed to appear, **Virarajendra occupied the kingdom**; unable to bear this final humiliation, and overtaken by a serious illness, **Someswara I, on 28th March C.E. 1068, went with a musical instrument to the Tungabhadra river and committed suicide by jumping into it.** Many inscriptions record his death, but Someswara I is remembered as the one ruler who got involved in incessant fighting with four emperors.

### Someswara II (1068 – 1076 A.D.)

After Someswara I, his son Someswara II carried on the rule from C.E. 1068 to 1076, with the title "**bhuvanaikamalla**."

*   Soon after his accession, Chola–Chalukya conflict started again. His brothers **Jayasimha** and **Vikramaditya VI** occupied Nolambavadi and Banavasi areas and rebelled against him. Chola **Virarajendra** invaded the Chalukyan kingdom; the Chalukyan cavalry force defeated the Chola armies and saved the Gutti fort.
*   **Cause → Effect:** When Someswara kept his younger brother Vikramaditya VI in charge of protecting Gangavadi, the latter — having an eye on the Chalukyan throne — rebelled against his elder brother, defeated him, and, as stated in Bilhana's _Vikramankadeva Charita_, occupied the kingdom.

### Vikramaditya VI (1076 – 1126 A.D.)

Younger brother of Someswara II and son of Someswara I; got coronated at Kalyani and ruled from C.E. 1076 to 1126 — considered a great king among the Western Chalukyas. His court poet **Bilhana's** _Vikramankadeva Charita_ gives details of his reign.

*   In the very first year of his reign, the **Salivahana era in vogue until then was changed and the Vikrama era was started in its place** — thus the **Chalukya Vikrama era** commenced from C.E. 1076.
*   Though Kalyani remained his capital, to improve the popular system of administration, different towns such as Vijayapuram and Vikramapuram were developed as important sub-category towns. Frequently moving about in these towns, he maintained peace and had high popular respect; administration attracted popular favour.
*   When his younger brother Jayasimha tried to rebel in C.E. 1080, it was suppressed. Aiming to occupy areas of the kingdom, the administrator of Vengi was defeated.
*   During his time, **Vishnuvardhana** of the Hoyasala dynasty occupied some parts of the kingdom, passing through Uchchangi and Belvala areas; the Hoyasalas occupied territory up to the river Krishna. Taking advantage of this, administrators of other feudatory kingdoms tried to rebel.
*   During his time, poets **Bilhana and Vijnaneswara** were patronised. Historians state that during his reign there was progress in all fields. He held the title "tribhuvanamalla."

### Someswara III (1126 – 1138 A.D.)

After Vikramaditya VI, his son Someswara III ruled the kingdom from C.E. 1126 to 1138. He wrote the work _Abhilashitardhachintamani_, described as "vijnanasarvasvam" (encyclopedia), also called "manasollasam."

Soon after becoming king, he took Banavasi and Gangavadi regions from the feudatories into his own control. But during his time only, the Vengi kingdom defied the supremacy of the Kalyani Chalukyas.

### Jagadekamalla (1138 – 1151 A.D.)

During his time, the Hoyasalas rose in power. He was the son of Someswara III. After Jagadekamalla, his younger brother **Tailapa III (C.E. 1151–57)** assumed authority.

### Decline and End of the Kalyani Chalukyas

Tailapa III's reign period was filled with wars against feudatory kings. By that time, **Kalachuri Bijjala**, discharging the duties of a minister, had grown stronger and secured the cooperation of feudatory kingdoms.

*   The minister of Bijjala was **Basaveswara**, the famous religious reformer; Bijjala favoured Jainism.
*   **In C.E. 1157, Kalchuri Bijjala drove away Tailapa III**, who left the capital and fled.
*   When the son of Tailapa III, **Someswara IV**, came to the capital Kalyani in C.E. 1183, **Ballala III**, the Hoyasala ruler, defeated him and drove him away. Someswara, for some time, lived in exile, and died at last in **C.E. 1200**.

**With this, the Kalyani Chalukyan dynasty has ended.**

In the Chalukyan age, Coastal Andhra remained under Vengi, and integrated Western Andhra feudatory dynasties used to rule. These feudatories, while cooperating with their sovereigns in waging wars, began to rule their kingdoms independently; their courts resembled those of the emperor, and they maintained councils of ministers.

Rejecting considerations of country, caste and family, and becoming selfish, feudatories fought among themselves for the throne; among them, Bhimasaluki and Yuddhamalla did not hesitate even to mortgage the country's independence. At that time armies roamed about freely; Vengi, Dharanikota, Nellore and Khammam got destroyed many times, and many villages were burnt — "there is no exaggeration in stating that the entire country got turned into a big war camp."

From another angle, some kingdoms flourished in a golden age (the Vemulavada Chalukyas). The administrative, economic and religious systems, social-life policy, architecture and sculpture, language and literature, and patronage of fine arts that developed during Chalukyan rule (sixth to twelfth century) in South India remained as **models for later dynasties** — the impact of these varied developments spread deeply into people's lives and progress.

### Emperor, Power, Status

Chalukyan government was a **hereditary monarchy**; the king was all in all. Kingly authority consisted of seven items (_saptanga_): king, minister, kingdom, treasury, army, friend and fort. In running the administration, the king was assisted by the **yuvaraja** (crown prince), also called **Uparaja**; kings without sons used to appoint their brothers or their brothers' sons as yuvaraja.

Chalukyan kings used titles such as "parameswara," "paramabhattaraka," "parama maheswara," "prithvivallabha," "Bhuvanasraya," "Rajadhiraja" and "rajaparameswara." Though the emperor was all-powerful, custom required him to rule according to the **dharmasastras**. Though a gap existed in this age between the king and the people, the duties of the emperor consisted of:

*   Protecting the people
*   Solving disputes among the people and delivering justice
*   Maintaining law and order in the country
*   Saving the kingdom from external invasions

For discharging these duties, the emperor arranged the **mantrimandali** (council of ministers).

### Council of Ministers

For helping the emperor in administration, the council of ministers was formed. It included those who knew the dharmasastras, the commanders-in-chief of the army, and important relatives of the king. The **minister, commander-in-chief, treasurer, purohit and yuvaraja** used to advise the king in administration.

*   These posts were generally held by men who observed dharma, could be trusted, were of good character, and were brahmins well versed in the knowledge of dharmasastras. They held these posts **hereditarily**.
*   During the Chalukyan times, these posts were gradually also held by Sudras. It is also learnt that these posts were held, as per ancient moral codes, by the "eighteen tirthas" of Sapthangas.
*   In the Vemulavadi inscription of Arikesari II, employees known as "mahasandhivigraha," "tantrapala" and "Satradipala" are mentioned. Employees referred to as "niyogadikrutha" and "niyogavallabha" perhaps served as supervisors of departments. It could be said that the **bahattara (72) niyogadhipaties** found in Kakatiya inscriptions might have been the descendants of these earlier officials. These employees received land grants as honorarium for their services.

### Local Government

Chalukyan administration to some extent resembled that of the Cholas.

**Administrative divisions:**

| Unit | Head |
|---|---|
| Rashtra (province) | Rashtradhipati |
| Vishaya (also called Nadu) | Vishyadhipati |
| Village | Gramani |

*   For administrative convenience, the empire was divided into provinces, and provinces were divided into **vishayas** (also called _nadus_): Kammanadu, Prolanadu, Attilinadu and Venginadu were among the names of local government units. In Rayalaseema, names like Seemanadu are found; in Southern Andhra, rashtras were called "Kottalu" — mentioned in the inscriptions of Pulinadu, located as Perumbagapadi.
*   It is learnt from inscriptions that there were **thirty vishayas in Venginadu**.
*   Local government was, to a great extent, in the hands of feudatory kings. In **Yellamanchilli, Pithapuram and Mudigonda**, only kings of Chalukyan dynasties assumed authority; besides them, the **Pattavardhani, Durjaya and Haihayadi** feudatory dynasties also rose.
*   **Village was the foundation of the administrative system.** A Grama sabha used to be there in every village; the village system attained a stable shape during the time of the Eastern Chalukyas. **Gramikas** were the important village officers during the time of the Rashtrakutas.
*   The Machilipatnam inscription of Chalukya Bhima II informs that village administration was carried out through committees; important decisions in village affairs used to be taken in the presence of village officers. Even emperors, when making land grants in villages, used to take their permission. Grama sabhas existed in Renadu; during their time, **Karanams** used to maintain village accounts. It is learnt through inscriptions that in Kunganoor, a person named Adavallam was appointed Karanam by the Grama sabha.

### Kingdom's Income and Expenditure

**Sources of income**

*   Tribute paid by feudatories to the kings was the main source of income for the Chalukyan government.
*   Some villages decided a yearly tax for the entire village rather than individual taxes — a method known as **"gramvar."**
*   Along with land tax, several other kinds of taxes existed; taxes could be paid either in cash or in kind. **Land tax amounted to 1/6th of the produce.** The word "sarvakarapariharam," used at the time of granting agraharas, indicates the wider tax net.
*   During the reign of **Trinetrudu**, king of Vaidumba, in Renadu, it is recorded that taxes on farmers such as _degaracha_ tax, _padevalu pannu_, _padiyeri pannu_ and _Sandhivigraha_ tax were removed.
*   Taxes such as _Kallavakkam, Vidanali Vishaya Sunkam, biradayam_ and _chittavatam_ are seen in Rayalaseema inscriptions.
*   The **Koravi inscription** issued by Niravadya, the Mudigonda Chalukyan king (C.E. 935), records that in Telangana, taxes were collected by kings from village leaders as a fixed or contractual amount; fines levied on criminals and other miscellaneous taxes could be collected by the village leader.
*   The **Vaidumba "Irugaya maharaju" inscription** (Vayalpadu Taluka, Chittoor district) records that village leaders such as _rattodi_ and _rattagudi_ could pay the king taxes such as _dogaraja_ tax, _padevali_ tax, _padiyeri_ tax and _sandhivigraha_ tax, while other miscellaneous taxes could be taken by the leaders themselves — _dogaraja_ tax was for the maintenance of the yuvaraja; _padevali_ tax was collected for maintaining the army; _sandhivigraha_ tax was for protecting the kingdom from enemy attack.
*   The Chevuru copper inscription of Eastern Chalukyan ruler Ammaraja I (C.E. 935) informs that, while appointing a village official for Mumikili village, it was laid down that eight _gadyanas_ paid for the endowment of the _gramani_ had to be paid to the king only, and the remaining miscellaneous taxes need not be paid by the gramani.
*   Employees decided the additional tax to be paid during the crop season, depending on the produce; **Rachakaranas** and **Rachasettis** collected this. Professional taxes were also levied — potters, washermen, barbers, goldsmiths and blacksmiths had to pay professional taxes. Chalukyas also received revenue from taxes on water-drawing machines, house tax, oil-mill tax, cattle tax, sheep tax, and market tax.

**Expenditure**

*   Chalukyan kings spent income from taxes on the army, royal family maintenance, salaries and allowances of employees, welfare activities, and charities and philanthropy.
*   It is learnt from Sukra's _Neetisaram_ that a king always had to keep **1/6th** of income in the treasury; of the remaining income, **half was to be spent on the army**, **1/12th on royal family expenses**, **another 1/12th on salaries and allowances of employees**, **another 1/12th on people's welfare**, and the **last 1/12th on charities and philanthropy**.
*   Public welfare activities of the time included: construction and maintenance of temples, patronage of poets/scholars/artists, development of educational activities, construction and maintenance of irrigation tanks, donations and charities, performance of sacrifices and rituals, and donations to religious institutions and mattahas.

### Judicial Administration

Clear information is not known about the judicial organisation followed by the Chalukyan rulers, though some inscriptions give references.

*   **The king remained the chief justice of the kingdom.** Judgments were given by "rashtradhipati" in provinces and "vishayapati" in vishayas; in villages, Grama sabhas gave judgments. Ordinary disputes were decided entirely in gramasabhas.
*   There were special judges called **"pradvivakas."** When disputes occurred between villages over land borders or use of water from a river, kings had them resolved through the pradvivakas, their ministers, or caste elders. These courts followed principles recorded in ancient Smriti works such as the **Yajnavalkya Smriti**.
*   Judgments delivered by these courts were issued under the king's emblem and in the name of "jayapatras." Special officers called **"mudravartulas"** were responsible for stamping the emblem.
*   The **Koravi copper-plate inscription (C.E. 935)**, considered the first Telugu inscription, gives details of the criminal investigation procedure followed under the Chalukyas. **"Mitakshara" of Vijnaneswara** and **"Neetikavyamruta" of Somadevasuri** are referred to as the dharmasastra works of the age. **"Smritisangraha,"** otherwise known as "Saraswathi Vilasam," written by "Prataparudragajapati" (a contemporary of the Yelamanchili Chalukya family), also informs about the justice and judicial codes of the Chalukyan times.
*   Only kings had the right to protect dharma and punish criminals; though the king was at the apex of the judicial system, in many parts of the kingdom he established courts and appointed judges. According to the Kollipara copper-plate inscription, **Arikesari I**, as a judge, established a court named **"dharma sabha."** According to "Saraswati Vilasam," members of the dharmasabha, numbering 3, 5 or 7, knowing the Vedas and judicial codes, were ordained to be truthful and impartial. Membership was denied to those with no knowledge of the kingdom's traditions and sastras, and to those known for cruelty.
*   Even guilds had special courts. As stated in "Vaisya purana," opposing the wrong decisions of king "Rajamahendravara," the vaisyas of 18 towns got organised into a **"vaisya sangha."**
*   Responsibility for preventing village thefts belonged to a village official called **Talari** — the leading servant of the village, also called village Police, pattilaka, pattera and Patel. His duty was to catch the thief and hand him over to the concerned legal authority; if he failed to catch the thief, he had to pay the cost of the stolen articles himself. This method was known as **"atchukavali."**
*   During Chalukyan times, **death sentence was the highest punishment**. At some places, though the intensity of punishment to brahmins was lessened somewhat, they never escaped punishment entirely. Depending on the degree of offence, punishments included: cutting of hands and legs, cutting of ears and nose, cutting the fore-part of the fingers of hands and legs, and burning the body in flames.
*   If a court employee committed a wrong, he was removed from post and his sources of income lessened — such an incident occurred in Pabubarru village, donated by Saktivarma, when a gramani who failed to obey the king's orders was removed from post. Basing on this, the Mudigonda and Vengi Chalukyas followed the codes of Saktivarma: if a person killed another, **120 drammas** was levied as penalty; if a person caused physical harm to another, **60 drammas** was imposed. If the modesty of a lady was attacked, a fine of **25 drammas** was imposed. As per the Srimadhavigeya maharaja inscription of Vaidumba king Bhuvanatrinetra, in cases of sexual atrocities, punishment was imposed on both men and women — males were fined **64 gadyanas**, and for women, **the nose used to be cut**. On the whole, punishments remained hard.

### Military Organisation

Chalukyan emperors used to personally lead their armies during wars, even while maintaining well-trained commanders-in-chief. **Kshatriyas** became famous as soldiers of courage and bravery. Because of constant Chalukya–Pallava–Chola–Rashtrakuta–Kalyani Chalukya conflicts, the need for soldiers increased, and persons of courage and bravery from **all castes** were taken and appointed as soldiers and commanders-in-chief.

*   Because of wars, a greater portion of the income received (from taxes and war loot) was spent on army maintenance. Chalukyan feudatory chiefs used to come, as and when needed, with their own armies to wage wars for the protection of the Chalukyan kingdom — hence it was said that the **main strength of the Eastern Chalukyan kingdom lay in the forces of their feudatory chiefs**.
*   Foot soldiers, elephant force and naval force were the main organs of the army. The **Aihole inscription of Pulakesi II** gives details of **six types of army organisations**:
    1.  **Mula** — the hereditary force
    2.  **Bhritya** — those who accompanied soldiers
    3.  **Sreni** — guild-based feudatory forces
    4.  **Mitra** — armies of friendly kingdoms
    5.  **Atavika** — forces of forest-based tribes
    6.  **Amitra** — captured forces
*   Army employees were called **"mahabaladhikruta"** (Great Commander-in-Chief). Forts were under the control of the **"durgadhipathi,"** who bore full responsibility for the protection of the fort — some army units were under his control. For army maintenance, either the wealth of the emperor or the income from villages was allotted.

### Agriculture, Irrigation, Crops, Land Revenue, Other Taxes

During the Chalukyan period, people's dependence on land and agriculture increased — a development that had begun after the Satavahanas. Brahmins, associated with temple service, were given lands and agraharas and turned into landlords; Sudras cultivated their lands and remained loyal to them. As pressure on land grew, expansion of agriculture became inevitable, and uncultivated and forest lands were converted into crop lands.

*   For tax purposes, agricultural lands were divided into different types: **low-lying/wet lands, dry lands, sandy lands (garuvu) and garden lands.** Land tax was fixed depending on water facility, land fertility and crop yield.
*   Chalukyan-era inscriptions reference commercial crops such as coconut, betel leaf, betel nut, mango, sugarcane, cotton, grams and pulses.

**Irrigation**

*   Emperors took steps to construct tanks and wells, and dig canals to pool water resources for agriculture. Rich people, feudatories and wealthy farmers helped construct and maintain tanks.
*   The **Chaita tank** and **Bhimasamudram** tank, mentioned in the Tadikonda inscription of Ammaraju II, still supply water to cultivated lands today.
*   A Western Chalukya inscription mentions a big tank called **Ananta Sarovaram** in Chebrolu (Guntur district). A Mahaboobnagar district inscription mentions a tank called **Bhimasamudram**. A big tank existed in Nalgonda district, under which 12 nivartanas of land were donated to brahmins. In Medak district, a tank known as **"madivojanakare"** existed. Feudatories of Kullottunga Rajendra II dug the **Polinayaka** and **Potta** tanks.
*   For those who brought new lands under cultivation, tax exemption was given in the beginning for some years, encouraging agriculture. Garden lands and light-soil lands were donated to temples — e.g., for _akhanda deepa_ maintenance at the Bheemeswara temple, Draksharamam, a garden of 2000 betel-nut trees was donated; a mango garden for the deity in Penta village (Nizamabad district) and one more mango garden for the temple at Bapatla were also donated.

**Land rights and taxes**

*   Every landlord had full authority over his land for donation, buying and selling, though acceptance from concerned village elders had to be obtained before taking these up. Nobody could hold personal rights over **banjar land**.
*   When land was donated, the extent of tax exemption given was known through **"sarvakara Pariharam"** — meaning exempted from all taxes.
*   On occasion, when kings and feudatories made donations depending on need, there was a custom of buying private individuals' lands and giving them to the donee.
*   Land tax related terms: **Ari** — tax paid after change of crop; **Siddhayam** — tax that had already been levied whether or not the crop came up; **taggu, tere** — other agriculture-related taxes.
*   Grain measurements in use: nivartana, martu, khandika, putti; even today in Telangana, measures such as putted manika and sola exist. For land measurement, there were "gedalu" (possibly wooden sticks) known as rajamana, mummidibhimakola, Janakola and rajarajakola.
*   Crop conditions, types and rain relationships were explained in a work known as **"sasyananda."** Writers such as **Somadevasuri** opined that taxes should not be collected before crops ripened and armies should not be quartered on crop lands — failing this would destroy the kingdom.
*   **King Vijayaditya's tax schedule** for lands in Malliswaradeva town (Vengi mandalam):

| Land Type | Tax (per putti) |
|---|---|
| Oodpu paddy field | 2 chinnas |
| Oodpu field | 6 chinnas |
| Dry land | 4 chinnas |
| Jowar land | (damaged in inscription — unknown) |
| New land | 2 chinnas |
| Gingelly land | (not preserved in inscription) |

Basing on such schedules and land productivity, tax used to be fixed; concessions were given for newly-cultivated lands, and animal husbandry was also encouraged.

### Industries

Chalukyan-era inscriptions show industries, trade and commerce were in good condition — industries allied to agriculture, jewellery-making, vehicle- and object-manufacturing, and smaller craft-based industries all existed.

*   Most agricultural-era wealth was spent on wars, luxuries and pomp; only a smaller portion went to production and welfare programmes. The administration settled craftsmen in villages by giving craft land grants and tax exemptions — villagers manufactured land-tilling implements (arakalu), cots, benches and low-seat armless single-seaters (peetalu). Iron ploughs and earthenware pottery were also made.
*   An inscription from the Draksharamam area shows **Teliki** (oil-extractor), **potterer, blacksmith, carpenter, maker of brass utensils (kanchari), and basket maker (medari)** were given tax-free lands.
*   Cloth industry continued through the period; thin, delicate fabrics were made for emperors and queens, while thicker woven cloth served common people. Implements and vessels were made with great skill in all metals, from gold to iron. Most villages had oil presses (ganugulu) and weaving looms.

### Trade and Commerce

Trade and commerce flourished during the Chalukyan age, though industry remained largely confined to rural needs. Powerful trade guilds carried on brisk trade, mostly in weapons for emperors and armies, luxury articles for the wealthy, spices, perfumes, diamonds, pearls, crystals, precious stones, and finely textured cloth.

*   Barter continued at a high level in villages, while coins circulated in towns. **Powerful merchant guilds** emerged; inscriptions record that vaisyas, telula (oil-pressers), perikas and balejas had their own guilds. Huge wealth came to the government through these guilds in the form of taxes and levies.
*   Fairs and pilgrimage places developed into trade centres — the fair at **Konidesa** used to run every Thursday.
*   Business was mainly in the hands of the **vaisyas**, called _nakarams_; every nakara had a _sreshti_. **Penugonda** became a leading trade city with 18 leading cities in the Vengi kingdom as central points. **Vengi, Ghantasala, Visakhanagaram and Nidadavolu** were trade centres. The **Ahadanakara inscription** informs about trade-guild activities. **Prithvivallabhapatnam** was considered a leading port town of the time.
*   The presence of Eastern Chalukyan coins in **Burma and Siam** testifies to continental trade. Many Andhra port towns were given Tamil names during this period: **Visakhapatnam** was named **Kulottunga Cholapattanam**, **Ghantasala** was named **Chola Pandyapuram**, and **Motupalli** was named **Deseeyakonda pattanam**.

**Coinage**

*   Currency in usage: **gadyana, mada, panam, kalamju, dramas** — denoting gold, silver and copper coins.
*   As per **Pavuluri Mallanna's** work, the relations between different coins were:

| Conversion |
|---|
| 4 gokara kanulu = 1 sorakani |
| 4 sora kanulu = 1 pittha |
| 4 pitthalu = 1 kani |
| 4 kanulu = 1 visam |
| 4 visalu = 1 pattika |
| 4 pattikalu = 1 chinnam |
| 4 chinnalu = 1 madha |

*   Besides coins, liquid measures (sola, manika, adde, kuncham) and solid measures (tulam, seru, veese, manugu, putti) were also in use.
*   **Trade guilds never sold all goods** — each guild sold only one commodity; those selling a particular commodity formed themselves into a guild, and only they could sell that commodity. On goods brought for sale, name-duty and place-duty were imposed; tax existed on salt and on cattle sold, collected only by officials. In the name of "Kolpuveesalu," a **Kolagaram tax** existed; when grain and other goods were measured, a duty was taken out of the total measured.
*   **Vedic religion did not allow sea voyage**, so Chalukyas did not carry on much foreign trade directly. Goods came in Chinese ships from Eastern countries and East Indies, and goods of the time were carried back in the same ships. Eastern Chalukyas sent ambassadors to Burma and China and maintained friendly relations with them, though foreign trade remained limited. Some locally-grown commodities and manufactured cloth were exported; horses and spices needed for emperors were imported from foreign countries. **Pavuluri Mallanna**, of the 12th century, gave the prices of commodities in his work "Sarasangrahaganitam."

To know about social conditions of the Chalukyan period, their inscriptions prove useful. **Vedic Brahman religion gained prominence and the varna system took stable shape.** Protection of _varnasrama dharma_ went on well during their rule.

*   Migrations as per occupation, regional bases, and the influence of different religions caused divisions to crop up in many castes. At this stage, there was **social uplift** in the lifestyle of people at the lowest rungs of the social ladder. From this age onward, people had freedom to make charities as per their desire. **Sanskrit education**, unlike earlier times, was made open to all from this age. Each caste's people had freedom to make necessary alternatives or additions to their caste regulations. Social customs and festivals varied from caste to caste — inscriptions giving information regarding the honour and status of different castes are seen in this period, though details on marriage relations and inter-dining between different castes and varnas are not clearly known.

### Brahmins

In the Chalukyan four-fold varna system, **brahmins held first place**, remaining at the top of society because of their Sanskrit education, study of Vedas and Vedangas, and service as teachers.

*   Reference to them is found in all royal-dynasty inscriptions; many emperors gave them agraharas — a system personally started by **Pulakesi II**. In Chalukyan age, all the ministers and dandanayakas who stood by the ruling dynasties belonged to the brahmin community only. Depending on gotra and pravara branch, there were divisions even among brahmins, identified as per the areas or centres in which brahmin families resided.
*   Due to discontent established in religious and political fields, royal patronage, and personal or family difficulties, brahmin families since the **9th century A.D.** started migrating; rulers provided arrangements for their stay. During Chalukyan times, in the Ghantasala area, house sites were given to **2000 brahmin families**.
*   More than their supposed eminence, their place in society came to be recognised because of their respected profession; countless agraharas are referenced in inscriptions given for maintaining items related to Vedic education and their livelihood.

### Kshatriyas

Many battles took place during the Vengi Chalukyan period, needing many soldiers for wars. **These kshatriyas went as soldiers at the time of wars and fought.** Those kshatriyas who considered administrative duties their responsibility came to be described as of "warrior varna."

*   From the Chalukyan time onward, **all categories of people began to participate in all kinds of activities**. To claim equal status with the old kshatriyas, every caste's people, from Chalukyan times, began to derive their origin from some pristine Purana Personality, and following this, as stated in inscriptions, members began to claim themselves of **lunar dynasty (Chandravamsa)** and **Surya vamsa (solar dynasty)**. The idea was prevalent that whoever performed kshatriya dharma or duty was kshatriya alone.

### Vysyas

In the Four-fold varna organisation, vaisyas formed the third group; their occupation was trade. They were called **sreshti, setti and komati**. Being devotees of Gomateswara (Jainism), they were also called _gomatlu_ or _komatlu_.

*   During Chalukyan times, trade and business were their occupation; organising into guilds and carrying on business both within and outside the country, they became rich. The fact that vaisyas could have their own armies for protecting their properties and providing security during trade journeys, and even giving loans to the administration itself, indicates their economic growth.
*   Vaisyas also had **born gotra names**. For their rights, they formed "**nakaram**" (nagaram); guilds worked to solve caste-related problems. Their caste goddess was **Vasavikanyaka** at Penugonda — there is no truth in the story mentioned in their "Kula puranam" that when a Chalukyan ruler tried to force her, she jumped into fire and died.
*   More than following administrators' orders, observing caste dharma and taking permission from caste elders for social activities was the prevailing norm.

### Sudras

Those belonging to the fourth group in the four-fold varna system came to be regarded as sudras. Just like other castes, many divisions emerged in their caste too, depending on occupation adopted for living, birth and regionalism — some took to agriculture, others adopted handicrafts.

*   During the Medieval age, many of those who took to military service happened to be sudra varna; their involvement was there in industries, handicrafts, and temple activities.
*   During Chalukyan times, opportunity came for some sudras to assume authority over the kingdom — Chalukya feudatories such as **Velanati kings, Kondapadamatlu, Tyagi and Parichchedi** all belonged to sudra caste only.
*   Contemporary historians state that people of craft-based occupations craved for social status; with the expansion of agriculture, their economic condition also gradually improved. The divisions among the sudras — **Velama and Kamma** — came as per regional divisions (Velanadu, Kammanadu); **Reddy**, in the first stage, was either a Rashtrakuta chief or Rattodi (an official of village administration) and gradually remained as the name of a division among the sudras.
*   As per Chalukyan-age inscriptions, in Edurupalli village near Draksharama, land grants were given separately to **teliki (oil-pressers), kammari (blacksmith), kamsali (carpenter), kanchari (makers of bronze articles)**, coconut and betel-nut gardeners, barbers, bronze workers, washermen, basket makers, and leather workers.
*   It is learnt from the organisation "sanimunnurvuru" that, just like people of other castes and occupations, **prostitutes also got organised into guilds** and led a movement for the protection of their rights, referred to in many inscriptions.

### Position of Women

In the patriarchal form of society prevalent during Chalukyan times, there was restriction on women, but they were "no impediment for the honour and status of women."

*   Though Smriti works and Jain works imposed restrictions and limitations on the freedoms of women, this need not be taken as reflecting contemporary realities — from politics to fine arts, there are many sources mentioning women's interference and participation.
*   Though marriage alliances did not generally occur between the Chalukya–Rashtrakuta dynasties, on other occasions, as **Chola princesses in succession married Chalukyan kings**, significant changes occurred in history. Because of queens such as **Kundavva, Ammangadevi and Madhurantaki**, it could be thought that Chola influence got established over the Vengi monarchy.
*   **Upper caste ladies and prostitutes used to earn skill in fine arts and other needed types of education.**

### Educational Organisation

In the Chalukyan age, religion-related Vedic studies received a lot of patronage. **Puranas, itihasas, dharmasastras, agamasastras, grammar, Vedanta, Astronomy, Diplomacy, Mathematics, Ayurveda and Logic** were studied.

*   In land-grant inscriptions, the rich knowledge of brahmin grant-receivers has been greatly described — in the Peddamaddali inscription, it is said that **Gupta Sarma** studied seventy commentaries on Logic alone. The Nidaparru inscription states that **Katte Sarma** thoroughly studied Vedas, itihasas, Puranas, dharmasastras and Upanishads; his grandfather, **Mandasarma**, was a scholar in Kalpa, purana, itihasa and dharmasastras at **Asanapura Ghatikasthana**.
*   Asanapuram became famous as a prominent **Ghatikasthanam** — the most eminent educational centre was called Ghatikasthanam. During Chalukyan times, **Ayurvedam, Dharmavedam, Gandharva and Arthasastras** used to be taught. Those who graduated from such Ghatikas were called **Ghatikasikas**.
*   **Rajaraja Narendra** stated he had studied Puranas, dharmasastras, kavyas and dramas, and had taken interest in Eashwaragamala. Educational learning mainly took place at **Agraharas, Brahmapurillu, Ghatikas, temples and matthas.** For traditional Sanskrit educational progress, agraharas remained as abodes given to scholars for patronising education and culture; sources state education was taught freely in agraharas, temples and matthas, and boarding/lodging facilities were provided.
*   **Nolambeswara temple in Hemavati** was a Ghatikasthanam; the **Hiresamudra inscription** mentions boarding arrangements provided for more than ninety students. Some educational centres had libraries — at **Nagai**, a big library was run, attached to an educational centre.
*   The educational system received financial help from the government, as well as cooperation and support from individuals, institutions and guilds. Some temples ran educational choultries.
*   Great effort was made in Mathematics during this period — **Pavuluri Mallanna**, who lived during Rajaraja Narendra's time, translated **"Ganitasastram"** written by **Mahaviracharya** (a Jain scholar), with the name **"Sarasangraha ganitam."** This work mentions the coins, tables and measurements in use at that time.

### Religious Developments

Among those who received Agraharas from the Chalukyan kings, brahmins — the basic pillars of Vedic religion — were greatest in number. During Chalukyan times, **Vedic religion was in the highest position**; **Kumarilabhattu**, who propagated _purvamimamsa Vedanta_ method, belonged to this age.

*   Because of self-reforms within Vedic religion, people's interest towards rituals and charities, idol worship, and construction of major temples increased. **Temple construction was taken up by the government as a movement and a social necessity.**
*   It became a tradition that the number of wars fought by Chalukyan kingdoms had to be equalled by the construction of an equal number of temples: **Vijayaditya II**, who waged **108 wars**, built **108 temples**; **Chalukya Bhima**, who waged **360 wars**, built **360 temples**.
*   The temple group at **Bikkavolu** was constructed during the time of Gunaga Vijayaditya; **Pancharamas**, prominent Saiva temples, were constructed during the time of the Chalukyas. A huge number of temples were built during the time of **Rajaraja Narendra**.
*   **Jataras** used to be held in temples — the _pradigam_ (procession) of idols was an important aspect. The Bezawada inscription (C.E. 930) of Yuddhamalla records that in Chebrolu, Mahasena's jatara procession was taken from Chebrolu to Bezawada.

### Saivism

Saivism had popular following during this period. In Saiva deeksha, **rudraksha, vibhuti and gurupadakam** (water from the feet of the teacher) formed main aspects; differences existed among Saiva branches regarding the manner of deeksha. A 7th-century inscription refers to "sivamandala deeksha."

*   At places like Vijayawada, propaganda known as "simha parishats" was established. **Srisailam, Alampuram and Draksharamam** had been exclusively Saiva centres; **Srisailam has been described by Bhavabhuti as a Kapalika centre.**
*   The temples built in the almost early stages of Chalukyan rule were all related to Saivism only. Siva was described as "mahavrati" by Nannechoda; Kapalika _vratam_ was only mahavratam. **Srisailam, Alampuram, Bezawada (Vijayawada) and Pithapuram** were the centres of Sakti worship of the day.
*   During this age, **Basaveswara (C.E. 1100–70)** in Karnataka started the **Vira Saiva movement**. Already before him, **Ekanta Ramaiah** and **Sripati Pandita** had propagated Virasaiva doctrines. It is said that, to prove the superiority of Siva, Ekanta Ramaiah got his head cut and received it back; Sripati Pandita (Vijayawada) kept fire in his upper garment ("uttariyam") to exhibit the superiority of Siva.
*   The idea that Siva was supreme deity, the wearing of _linga_ as an instrument of devotion, and the integration of _linga_ (idol) and _anga_ (body) had been chief aspects of Virasaivism, which was called "agamantam" (end of agama). After Basaveswara, **Mallikarjuna Pandita** propagated Saivism further — while going around the country, he exterminated Jains and Buddhists and propagated Saivism.
*   **Ammaraju II** donated Tadikonda village to Bhuvanasraya Siva temple in Vijayawada — on behalf of the Siva temple, this land grant was received by **Prabhutarasi**, a Saiva saint. Vemulavada Chalukyas also gave donations to Saiva saints; among them, **Arikesari I** donated Belmoga village to Sadyosivacharya as an educational grant.

### Vaishnavism

With the new vigour that came from the propagation of **Ramanuja**, Vaishnavism began to compete with Saivism. In the Chalukya–Chola age, there were many Dravida Vaishnava families. "**Keyurabahu Charithra**" informs that **Kommana** minister carried out Vishnu installation in **32 temple centres**. In Vaishnava deeksha, "Chakrankitalu," "Pundradharana," "Uchishista Bhojana," "dasanamadharana" and "ekadasivratam" had been main aspects.

*   During Chalukyan age, extremist movements sprang up for the sake of Saiva and Vaishnava faiths. **Ramanujacharya** imparted Vaishnava deeksha to lower-varna people but did not condemn the varna system. **Palanati Brahmanayudu** propagated Vira Vaishnavism.
*   Besides Virasaiva and Viravaishnava religions, over and above sectarian differences, the traditional **Smarta faith** also received encouragement. Vaishnava temples such as **Bapatla Bhavanaryana Swami temple, Sarpavarapu Bhavanarayanaswami Temple and Mandvya Narayanaswamy temple at Samarlakota** attained prominence during the Chalukyan time.

### Buddhism

It is learnt through the biography of Panditaradhya that Buddhists lived in Chandole area. From the sentence "Chaityamatynatam yatra nana chitrasuchitatvam," found in Amaravati inscriptions, it is understood that the **Dhanyakataka Chaitya did not suffer loss**, but Buddha, as an incarnation of Vishnu only, was getting worshipped — this is also stated in inscriptions at Amaravati, Karimnagar and Bikkavolu.

The name-sake Buddha worship, as a result of extremist Saiva propaganda by Panditaradhya, got ended; after the 5th and 6th centuries C.E., Buddhism began declining in the region.

### Jainism

Inscriptional sources record that **Jainism was patronised** during the time of the Badami, Vengi and Kalyani Chalukyas.

*   **Ayyanamahadevi**, queen of Kubjavishnuvardhana, established **Nedumba Vasadi** at Bezawada and donated Mushinikonda village to it.
*   **Ammaraju II**, at the request of his wife "Chamakamba," donated "Kalachumbarru" village to the Jains; at the request of **Durgaraju**, head of Karmarashtra vishaya, he gave many donations for constructing Katakabharana Jina temples. Further, Ammaraju II, at the request of his commanders-in-chief **Bhima and Naravahana**, gave Pedagadelaparru village for constructing Jina temples at Bezawada.
*   **Ramathirtham, Bikkavolu, Hanumakonda, Potlacheruvu, Kolanupaka (Nalgonda) and Vardhamanapuram** were prominent Jain centres. **Vemulavada**, the capital of the Vemulavada Chalukyas (feudatories of the Rashtrakutas ruling in present Telangana), and their early capital, **Podanapuram (Bodhan)**, were also leading Jain centres — at **Potlacheruvu (Patan Cheruvu)** alone, there were around **500 Jain Vasadis** (places of stay for Jain monks).
*   **Vimaladitya**, the Vengi Chalukya king, also patronised Jainism, adopting it toward the end of his rule. During the time of **Anantavarma Rajarajadeva**, who ruled Kalinga in C.E. 1178, a merchant named Kannamanayaka built the Rajaraja Jina temple at Bhogaram village (Visakhapatnam district) and made land grants to it. **Danavulapadu** in Jammalamadugu Taluk developed as a great Jain temple centre.
*   During Vemulavada Chalukya times, **Yuddhamalla Jina temple at Sanigaram, Baddega Jina temple at Vemulavada (Subhadama jina temple), and Arikesari Jina temple at Repaka** were constructed. At Bodhan, it seems there was earlier a statue of Gomattheswara; seeing this, **Chamundaraya**, minister of Rachamalla Gangaraju, installed the idol of Gomattheswara at **Sravanabelagola** in Karnataka around C.E. 970–990.
*   **Somadevasuri**, a Jainacharya with the Vemulavada kings, was a great scholar who wrote **"Yasastilaka"** — a champu kavya, also called **Yasodhara Charitra** — and **"Neetikavyamrutam."** For him, king Baddega built a famous Jain temple, the **Subhadama Jina temple**, at Vemulavada; for its maintenance, **Arikesari III** donated the village **Vanikatupalli**.
*   **Pampa**, the poet, in his "Vikramarjuna Vijayam," also gave an account of Jain Tirthankaras. **Jinavallabha**, brother of Pampa, was himself a Jain devotee — he issued an inscription stating he had the statue of the Jain goddess **Chakreswari** carved on a hillock near Kurkyala village (about 20 km from Karimnagar) and held celebrations there.
*   **Hanumakonda** is one of the ancient Jain temple centres in Telangana. On the present-day **Padmavathi hillock**, images of the Jain Tirthankaras Parsvanatha and Sasanadevi are found. In Jain Sangha, both _yathulu_ (monks) and _upasakulu_ (laity) existed; among Jains, divisions such as **Sangha, Gana, Gachha, Bali and Anya** existed. Educational learning of Jains started with the principle "Om namah Siddhamnamah" — it is the opinion of some that, by adding "Sivayanamah," this was later turned into a Jain principle.

### Literary Development

**Telugu language**, which till then remained "like a forest tree in unknown state," started from the time of the Chalukyas to develop into a tree blossoming with leaves, flowers and fruits. The great literary movement that started in this age went on progressing; most Telugu inscriptions of the Chalukya–Chola age are in verse form, and every verse inscription turned out to be a masterpiece.

*   As per the **Chebrolu inscription**, the nature of literary industry and the fact that in those days _marga_ and _desi_ literary styles were prevalent in Telugu are known. **Nannechoda** was the greatest prevalent poet of the age; as far as known in Telugu, **he was the first poet honoured by the royal dynasty**, holding the title "Kavirajasekhara" for his "Kumarasambhavam."
*   The influence of Kannada language and literary tradition was high; **Prakrit** remained the state language during Satavahana and Ikshvaku times, and from the time of the Vishnukundins, **Sanskrit** became the state language, with Telugu remaining only the medium of the common people's matters. **For the first time, it was the Eastern Chalukyas who gave the honour of official language to Telugu.**
*   Though Sanskrit inscriptions were more numerous during their period, the Chalukyas also issued inscriptions in Telugu. The **Telugu Chola** rulers, ruling the Renadu area, were the first to introduce the practice of getting royal inscriptions written in Telugu; the **Vipparla inscription of Jayasimhavallabha I** was the **first Eastern Chalukyan inscription** in Telugu. **Mallikarjuna Panditaradhya** wrote "Sivatatvasaram" — more than 400 kanda verses — recognised by scholars as a **Sataka**; hence, the credit for starting the "Sataka Prakriya" (style) in Telugu goes to Panditaradhya.
*   Among those who used the Telugu language were the **Renati Cholas, Western Chalukyas and their feudatories, and Bana kings**. In inscriptional Telugu of the first stage, all inscriptions were written in prose, and Prakrit words got mixed into Telugu extensively — e.g. the word "reddi" appeared as "rattagudi/rattadi/rattodi"; "purugulu" for "nasanam" (destroyer) appeared as "pruvullu"; "cheyuvadu" (rachuvasu) used to appear; plural indicators used "lu"; "gudulu" and "madulu" were called "gudlu" and "madlu"; "padamata" was uttered as "paruta"; and "Chola/Choda" was called "Chora."
*   There is something significant in the method of sentence formation: in inscriptions of our present-day sentence structure, subject comes first with some adjectives, then object and other words. A different sentence-writing style existed in the **Macherla inscription of Jayasimha Vallabha I** and the **Potladurthi–Malepadu inscription of Renati Cholas**.
*   By the time of **Gunaga Vijayaditya**, Telugu had come under Sanskrit's influence; poetry writing started with local metre, guided by matra and gana. **Taruvoja** in the inscription of Panduranga; "seesa verses" in the Kandukuru inscription; and "**madhyakkara**" in the Bezawada inscription (C.E. 930) are examples.
*   Gradually, Telugu language attained "**kavya**" shape; **Pampa**, who wrote "Vikramarjuna Vijayam" — the first "kavya" in Kannada — belonged to the age of the Chalukyas. Scholars opine **Tikkana Somayaji** was the greatest not only among the poets of the Chalukyan age but among all Telugu poets — his was a scholarly family. **Bhaskara mantri** wrote "Bhaskara Ramayananm." **Ketana**, who wrote "Kadambari" as a Telugu padya kavya, might have been Tikkana's elder father.
*   **Tikkana** was not only a great minister and poet — "he was a great cultural movement." He wrote "**Nirvachanottara Ramayana**," dedicated to Manumasiddhi. The works of **Palkuriki Somanatha** — "Panditaradhya Charitra" and "Basava Puranam" — won fame in Telugu. **Ketana**, who wrote "Dasakumar Charitra" and "Vijnaneswaram," and **Marana**, who wrote "Markandeya Purana," belonged to this age. **Narayanabhattu** helped Nannaya in writing "**Andhra Mahabharata**." In this way, the Chalukyan age contributed greatly to Telugu literary development.

### Art Development

Royal courts and temples of Chalukyan times were the centres for the arts of music, dance, architecture and sculpture. The early Chalukyas, at their capital Badami and its surrounding places, constructed many cave temples.

*   Prominent temples came up at **Aihole and Pattadakal** in Karnataka — as many as around **70 temples at Aihole** and **10 temples at Pattadakal** were constructed, exhibiting Chalukyan architectural and sculptural styles. These temples were built by erecting a rectangular platform over which a row of pillars was arranged to bear the roof load — walls were absent on the four sides, and this structure, called "**sandhagaram**," might have been used as a meeting place for village elders and people.
*   In Mahaboobnagar district (present-day Telangana), at **Alampur** on the bank of the sacred Tungabhadra river, there are **nine temples**, otherwise called the **Navabrahma temples**. Among them, six had compound walls; the remaining stay outside this compound wall. All nine temple names end with the word "brahma," but all these are actually **Siva temples**, with Siva lingas installed in them. Among these nine, "**Viswabrahma**" temple was the biggest; these temples still receive worship today.
*   Temples built at **Vemulavada** belonged to the ninth and tenth centuries. Among these, **Bhimeswara temple** is important — built by **Baddega**; it was earlier called "Baddegeswara" temple. At its sanctum-sanctorum entrance, a **Gajalakshmi** carving was placed; the walls of the sanctum sanctorum have four pillars — a tradition of the early Chalukyas.
*   At the **Bhimalingeswara temple** in Vemulavada, on the northern wall of the sanctum sanctorium, a sculpture of **"Mahishasura mardini"** was carved. **Nageswara temple** is another temple at Vemulavada, built during the time of Arikesari II — the god worshipped by merchants is called "Nagareswara," with a Siva linga installed in the inner temple. A Jain temple was built at Repaka by Arikesari III (per inscriptions). In Karimnagar district, 22 km from Manthena, beside "Adavisomnapalli" village, **four cave temples** exist.
*   In coastal Andhra, Eastern Chalukyas built many temples, displaying love for architecture and sculpture, showing the influence of Pallava-Chalukya traditions. **Vijayaditya II stated he built 108 temples.** Inscriptional evidence states **Gunaga Vijayaditya built the Vijayeswara temple at Bikkavolu**. **Chalukya Bhima** constructed **Bhimeswara temples at Draksharama**; the temples at **Bhimeswaram, Palakollu and Amaravati** (in Pancharamas) were also Chalukyan constructions. **Yuddhamalla** built the **Kumaraswamy temple** at Bezawada; **Mahadevi**, queen of Vikramaditya II, built a magnificent Saiva temple at Pattadakal to mark her husband's victories. At **Yeleswaram** in Nalgonda district, many old Siva temples emerged.
*   **Gunaga Vijayaditya** built **six temples at Bikkavolu**; among these, excepting the **Golingeswara temple**, all others are in ruined condition. **Golingeswara temple, Chandrasekhara temple and Rajarajeswara temple** were all built on a square plan, two to three storeys, with art and nagara-style vimanas — these were rebuilt in later times. **Rajarajeswara temple was built by Rajaraja Narendra.**
*   Music and dance were patronised in royal courts and temples. **Ammaraju** held the title "kavigayaka kalpataruvu." **Chalukya Bhima I** honoured **Challavva**, an adept in Gandharva Vidya, with a land donation; her father **Mallappa** was described as like Tumbura in the art of music. Sculptures of the age show musical instruments such as violin, flute, mrudangam (maddela) and talas. Names of dancers, musical-instrument players and dance teachers are found in inscriptions; several types of dance songs and different kinds of ragas (tunes) are recorded respectively in "Panditaradhya Charitra" and "Kumara Sambhavam."
*   Painting had great importance in Chalukyan age. Painting at **Badami** is called a beautiful specimen of Deccan painting; paintings in **cave temples two and three at Badami** (C.E. 578) are wonderful testimony to early brahmin painting. In sculptures at Vijayawada, Jammidoddi, and one found at Chebrolu, dance and instrumental "operas" are depicted. Among the pastimes of the period, **kolatam** — an admixture of dance and singing — was popular.

The period of Chalukyan rule could be considered a **glorious age in South Indian history**. Over their long period of rule — sixth to twelfth century — the Chalukyas achieved political unity and successfully resisted foreign invasions of South India; regarding the Arab invasion of Northern India during their time, they were able, to some extent, to prevent its spread to the western areas. Even though Chalukyan kings emerged from continuous wars, they developed South India in all fields and thereby could bring back memories of Satavahana rule.

*   The rule of **Chalukya Bhima**, who ruled from Vengi as capital, deserves special mention — during his time, the Bhimeswara temple at Draksharama and one more Bhimeswara temple at Chalukya Bhimavaram were built, and the fame of the Chalukyas was taken to greater heights. During their time, though Buddhism slid back, **Jainism flourished greatly**.
*   During the time of the **Badami Chalukyas**, Pulakesi II, as part of his military conquests, occupied most parts of Telangana and Rayalaseema and proclaimed the eminence of the Chalukyas. **Vemulavada Chalukyas**, who ruled over Telangana areas, gave the fruits of great administration to the people of Telangana — during the time of **Baddega**, who fought 42 battles without tasting defeat in any one of them, war heroes like him brought glory to the age. During the time of Vemulavada Chalukyas, **Arikesari II**, taking advantage of relations with the Rashtrakutas, was able to expand his empire. **Mudigonda Chalukyas** also, with the confidence of the Eastern Chalukyas, ruled over the Telangana region.
*   Though local government resembled that of the Cholas, the Chalukyas divided their empire into administrative units. A large percentage of state income was spent on people's welfare programmes, earning the people's admiration. In army maintenance too, new changes could take place — **Pulakesi II**, in the Aihole inscription, referred to the six types of army organisations. Keeping responsibility for catching criminals with local officials, and giving importance to village assemblies in judicial trials, remained useful and praiseworthy measures.
*   Giving importance to tank construction contributed to improving crop yields — the **Chaita tank** and **Bhima Samudram**, mentioned in the Tadikonda inscription of Ammaraju II, still supply water to cultivated lands today. Along with agriculture, industries, trade and commerce proceeded on a progressive path; weaving of different kinds of cloth gained importance among the handicrafts.
*   Though the four-fold varna system was prevalent, **sudras and women could freely take up their activities and enjoy their rights**. Saiva and Jain faiths enjoyed good patronage and progress — reflected in temples constructed at **Alampuram, Vemulavada, Kolanupaka, Aihole and Pattadakal**, which stand even today as specimens of Chalukyan architectural and sculptural style.
*   Next to Saivism and Jainism, Vaishnavism also gained importance and enjoyed patronage. In literary field, inscriptions and writings began in Prakrit and Sanskrit languages, and gradually — during the time of the Eastern Chalukyas and Vemulavada Chalukyas — **Telugu, the language of the local people, started becoming the medium for inscriptions and writings**; with the preparation of "Mahabharata" in Telugu by **Nannaya**, court poet of Rajaraja Narendra, the way became clear for the development of Telugu language and literature.

It could be realised that the Chalukyas, during their long rule of six centuries, could introduce **stable, praiseworthy, popular, ideal and trend-setting systems and changes** in political, administrative, economic, social and cultural fields. In that way, their rule period could be considered as an **age by itself** in Telangana as well as South Indian history, without any doubt.

Kubja Vishnuvardhana is believed to have died fighting alongside his brother Pulakesi II in a battle against which Pallava ruler?
The first Telugu inscription of the Eastern Chalukyas was issued during the reign of which ruler?
faqs.e: This inscription was issued at Vipparla village (Narasaraopet mandal, Guntur district).

faqs.q: Who succeeded Jayasimha I (Jayasimhavallabha I) and ruled for only seven days, issuing the Kondanagoor inscription?
Wars of succession began in the Eastern Chalukya dynasty from the time of which ruler?
Which Rashtrakuta ruler ended the Badami Chalukya dynasty around C.E. 755, marking the start of the second phase of Eastern Chalukya history?
During the reign of Vishnuvardhana IV, which Vemulavada Chalukya ruler was sent by Rashtrakuta Dhruva to defeat him?
Vijayaditya II fought 108 battles over twelve years with the help of which dynasty to occupy Vengi?
faqs.e: His commander was Nruparudra of the Haihaya dynasty; for these victories Vijayaditya II earned the titles "Narendreswara" and "Chalukyaraya," among others.

faqs.q: It is said that Vijayaditya II built how many Siva temples, one at each place he fought a battle?
Which town is said to have got its name because of Vijayaditya II?
Gunaga Vijayaditya (Vijayaditya III) took charge of the Pali dhvaja and which torana as symbols of Eastern Chalukya supreme authority?
Gunaga Vijayaditya appointed which brahmin commander-in-chief, who conquered Boya Kottas and held Nellore?
Gunaga Vijayaditya's authority extended from Mahanandi to which lake, marking the peak of Eastern Chalukya power?
Rashtrakuta king Krishna II, after being defeated by Gunaga Vijayaditya, accepted his sovereignty as recorded in which set of inscriptions?
Which Ganga king annexed the Trikalinga kingdom, taking advantage of the internal quarrels in the Vengi Chalukya dynasty after Gunaga Vijayaditya's death?

Consider the following statements regarding Gunaga Vijayaditya (Vijayaditya III):
(I) He was also referred to as Gunaka Vijayaditya.
(II) He conquered Gangavadi and Nolambavadi in C.E. 870.
(III) After his death, quarrels started in the Vengi Chalukya dynasty over the throne.
Which of the above statements is/are correct?
Chalukya Bhima I's accession was opposed by which uncle, who sought Rashtrakuta help?
Which Vemulavada king, insulted during Gunaga Vijayaditya's time, captured Chalukya Bhima in the war at Kolleru?
The Koravi copper-plate inscription (C.E. 935) informs that Chalukya Bhima made which relative his Dandanadha (commander-in-chief) to defeat the Rashtrakuta army?
faqs.e: Mahakala was the son of Chalukya Bhima's stepmother.

faqs.q: Chalukya Bhima I installed which temple at Draksharamam?
As per his own inscriptions, how many battles did Chalukya Bhima I wage during his 30-year rule?
Vijayaditya IV (Kollabhiganda) died in the Viraja battle fought against which ruler?

options.c: Vajrahasta III of Kalinga Ganga dynasty

faqs.a: Vajrahasta III of Kalinga Ganga dynasty

faqs.q: Which Eastern Chalukya ruler is credited with establishing Rajamahendrapuram as the Chalukyan capital?
faqs.e: As Vengi, being in a flat plain, was easily subjected to enemy attacks, Ammaraju established his capital on the northern coast of the Godavari, taking the title "rajamahendra."

faqs.q: Who drove away Yuddhamalla II and occupied the Vengi throne, killing his competitors Tatabikki, Rajamarthanda and others?
Ammaraju II's brother, who killed him and ascended the Vengi throne with the help of Rashtrakuta Krishna III and the Mudigonda Chalukyas, was:
Danarnava gifted away Pottapinadu to which dynasty, who had helped him?
Who attacked and killed Danarnava, declaring himself king and bringing Vengi political history into its "third stage"?
Danarnava's sons, Saktivarma and Vimaladitya, fled to Kalinga and later sought shelter from which dynasty against Jatachoda Bhima?
Chola king Rajaraja gave his daughter Kundavva in marriage to which Vengi Chalukya prince to strengthen ties?
In which year did Jatachoda Bhima die in battle near Kanchipuram against Saktivarma and the Chola army?
Saktivarma bore which title, coins of which were found on the Arakan coast?
Vimaladitya, though a Saiva in the beginning, later accepted which religion?
faqs.e: Desiganacharya, "trikalayogi" and "siddhantadeva" were his gurus at the time of his initiation; he built a cave temple called Ramakonda at Ramathirtham.

faqs.q:
Consider the following pairs regarding Vimaladitya's wives and their sons:
(I) Kundavva (Chola princess) – Rajaraja Narendra
(II) Melima (Telugu Choda princess) – Vijayaditya
Which of the pairs given above is/are correctly matched?
Who celebrated the coronation of Rajaraja Narendra on 16th August, C.E. 1022, after invading Vengi and defeating Vijayaditya?
Rajaraja Narendra's court poet, who began writing the Andhra Mahabharata in Telugu, was:
faqs.e: Nannaya, titled "sabdasasana," was assisted by Narayanabhattu; he completed the first two-and-a-half parvas of the work.

faqs.q: In which battle/war of C.E. 1053 did Chola Rajadhiraja die, resulting in Rajaraja Narendra having to accept Western Chalukya supremacy?
In which year did Vijayaditya (VII) die, marking the end of the Vengi Chalukya dynasty?
Rajendra, who finally joined Vengi to the Chola empire, ascended the Chola throne under which title?
Which Western Chalukya (Kalyani Chalukya) king foiled Chola efforts and established Kalyani Chalukyan dominance at Vengi following Jayasimha's death?

Consider the following statements regarding the end of the Vengi Chalukya dynasty:
(I) Rajendra Chola II tried to drive Vijayaditya VII from Vengi to restore Rajendra to his father's kingdom.
(II) Virarajendra conquered Vengi, Kalinga and Chakrakuta in C.E. 1067.
(III) Rajendra's army was defeated by Vijayaditya with the help of Rajraja Devendra Varma of Kalinga and Yasahkarnadeva, the Chedi king.
Which of the above statements is/are correct?
The Vemulavada Chalukyas ruled which region as feudatories of the Rashtrakutas?
Who is regarded as the founder of the Vemulavada Chalukyan kingdom, having served as commander-in-chief of Dantidurga?
Vinayaditya Yuddhamalla ruled with which city as his capital, before it was later shifted?
faqs.e: Dantidurga appointed him feudatory for the areas of Bodhan (Nizamabad) and Karimnagar in appreciation of his conquest of the Chitrakuta fort.

faqs.q: During the war of succession between Rashtrakuta Dhruva and Govinda II, which side did Arikesari I support?
As a mark of victory, Dhruva gifted Arikesari I areas in Nagarkurnool (Mahaboobnagar district) and which other district?
faqs.e: With this eastward extension, the Vemulavada Chalukya capital shifted from Bodhan to Vemulavada.

faqs.q: Which Vemulavada Chalukya ruler held the title "soladaganda," meaning a warrior who knew no defeat, after winning forty-two battles?

Consider the following statements regarding Baddega, the Vemulavada Chalukya ruler:
(I) He invaded Vengi and took Chalukya Bhima into custody.
(II) He was defeated by Kusumayudha of the Mudigonda Chalukya dynasty.
(III) He built a temple at Vemulavada known as the Baddegeswara temple.
Which of the above statements is/are correct?
faqs.e: The Baddegeswara temple is now famous as the Vemulavada Bheemeswara temple.

faqs.q: Narasimha II, feudatory of Rashtrakuta Indra III, defeated which Gurjara Prathihara ruler in his northern military expedition?
Narasimha II's wife, Jakavva, was the sister of which Rashtrakuta ruler, and became the mother of Arikesari II?
Which Vemulavada Chalukya ruler is most admired as a scholar, warrior, great organiser and patron of poets, during whose rule Pampa wrote "Vikramarjuna Vijayam"?
Arikesari II helped install which ruler, under the name Amoghavarsha III, on the Rashtrakuta throne after defeating Govinda IV?
In Vikramarjuna Vijayam, the poet Pampa compared Arikesari II to which epic hero?
faqs.e: Delighted with the work, Arikesari II gave Pampa Dharmapuri (Jagityal Taluka) as an agrahara.

faqs.q: Vegaraju, eldest son of Arikesari II, ruled with which town as his capital?
Baddega II (Bhadradeva) built a Jaina monastery of Gauda Sangha at Vemulavada, named:
Who was the last king of the Vemulavada Chalukya dynasty?
In which year did Arikesari III destroy the Rashtrakuta dynasty and establish the Kalyani Chalukya kingdom with Tailapa II as king?
faqs.e: Along with the Rashtrakutas, Vemulavada Chalukya rule also came to an end in 973 A.D.

faqs.q: Which temple built by the Vemulavada Chalukyas at their capital became famous as a Saiva temple of their time?
Which Jain scholar associated with the Vemulavada kings wrote "Yasastilaka" and "Neetikavyamrutam"?
Jinavallabha, brother of the poet Pampa, had the statue of which Jain goddess carved on a hillock near Kurkyala village?

Consider the following pairs of Vemulavada Chalukya rulers and their reign periods:
(I) Arikesari I – 775 – 800 A.D.
(II) Baddega – 850 – 895 A.D.
(III) Arikesari II – 930 – 955 A.D.
Which of the pairs given above is/are correctly matched?
The Mudigonda Chalukyas ruled over Manchikondanadu in Koraviseema, with which town as their capital?
The Khammam and Warangal areas together came to be known by which name during Mudigonda Chalukya times?
Who was the founder of the Mudigonda Chalukyan dynasty, acquiring Koravi mandalam with the help of the Eastern Chalukyas?
Kusumayudha (Kusumayudhudu), son of Ranamardhudu, freed which Vengi Chalukya ruler from Rashtrakuta Krishna II's captivity and installed him on the throne?
Gonagaiah, son of Kusumayudha, was named after which Eastern Chalukya ruler, out of regard for him?
faqs.e: Gonagaiah was also called Karigonaga ("black Gonaga"), being the short form of Gunaga Vijayaditya's name.

faqs.q: Who removed Gonagaiah and himself ascended the Mudigonda Chalukyan throne, as recorded by the Koravi inscription?
faqs.e: Having lost the kingdom, Gonagaiah sought the help of Arikesari II and, with his support, dethroned Niravadya to regain the Mudigonda kingdom.

faqs.q: Rashtrakuta king Krishna II appointed which commander-in-chief as administrator over Kurravadi, whose line eventually established the Kakatiya dynasty?
faqs.e: Gundaya, Yeriya's father, was a Rashtrakuta, referred to as Dandeva Gundana in the Machilipatnam inscription of Chalukya Bhima.

faqs.q: Which town did Yeriya make his capital, with which the Kakatiya dynasty was installed?
Which Vengi Chalukya ruler made Kakartya Gundana ruler of Natavadi and tried to send the Mudigonda Chalukyas to the Renati region?
Which Kalyani Chalukya ruler's commander, Viriyala Yerrabhupati, defeated Kakartya Gundana and installed Bottu Betadu as king in Koraviseema?
faqs.e: This is recorded in the Gudoor inscription (C.E. 1124).

faqs.q: Whose wife, Kamasani, felt sympathy for the minor Garuda Betaraju and sought Tailapa's help to restore the kingdom to him?
faqs.e: Tailapa gave the Hanumakonda area to Garuda Betaraju as part of this arrangement, stabilising both the Kakatiyas in Warangal and the Mudigonda Chalukyas in Koraviseema as feudatories of Tailapa II.

faqs.q: According to the Palampeta inscription, which Kakatiya ruler invaded the Mudigonda Chalukyas (feudatories of the Kalyani Chalukyas) and drove them away?
Who was the last ruler among the Mudigonda Chalukyas, as learnt from the Krivvaka inscription?
Which Kakatiya ruler invaded and defeated Nagatiraju, bringing the Mudigonda Chalukyan kingdom into the Kakatiya empire?

Consider the following statements regarding the sources for Mudigonda Chalukya history:
(I) The Koravi copper-plate inscription (C.E. 935) covers the period up to the Eastern Chalukyan age.
(II) The Viriyalavari Gudoor inscription (C.E. 1124) is a source for later Mudigonda Chalukya history.
(III) These inscriptions contain clear dates and adequate information, giving full clarity on Mudigonda Chalukya history.
Which of the above statements is/are correct?
faqs.e: Statement III is incorrect — as the inscriptions have no dates in places and inadequate information, there was limited opportunity to know their full history.

faqs.q: The Kalyani Chalukyas are also known by which alternate name?
Which two works, written by Meruthunga Charyulu, state that the Kalyani Chalukyas belong to Telangana?

What was the first capital of the Kalyani Chalukyas, before it was later shifted to Kalyani?
